你们总得用些陈词滥调来开场，而我认为组建团队最常见的陈词滥调就是“团队至上”对吧？如果你在听这个话题，可能听过无数次，也可能亲口跟别人说过，甚至接受过这方面的指导。但我在创业初期听到过这种说法，当时我觉得这建议糟透了。我当时以为产品或营销才是关键阻碍。但现在我认为，虽然团队确实至关重要——我深信这一点——但看看大多数公司的数据和行为，你会发现现实并非如此。（00:05:55）让我来谈两个根本问题。第一个问题是，我们把团队想得过于完美，试图迎合所有人，尤其是过去几年的科技行业。或许现在情况有所改善，但过去那种“每个人都要开心”的思维模式实在存在太久了。我觉得这是一种严重的误解，因为你不是为了取悦所有人而存在的。你有自己的使命和目标，团队文化也应该围绕这些核心价值来构建。

（00:06:24）更实际的解决方案是：我们根本没有真正关注团队。科技行业管理者的平均任期目前约为15.7个月。我之所以研究这个数据，主要是因为过去几年我们过度强调团队概念。企业科技领域员工与同一位经理共事的平均时长仅为10.8个月，接近11个月。团队至上根本站不住脚——当团队管理者自身的任期如此短暂时，又怎么能谈得上团队至上呢？

（00:06:57）而且我认为人力资源管理在很大程度上被视为事后补救措施。即便回顾人力资源发展的历史（这里不展开），它也始终以被动应对为主。它源自19世纪中叶的劳工运动，核心诉求是“如何规避法律风险”，而非“如何推动团队进步”。科技行业本有机会改变这种现状，但我们始终没有真正关注团队的使命。不知道我是否回答了你的问题，但我认为问题的核心在于：我们没有围绕使命真正关注团队。我们只是招人进来，期望他们开心而已。当然我这里是以偏概全，但从数据和现实来看，大多数公司确实如此。

(00:08:22): You also have different types of people that do better at the particular company than not. (00:08:53): So Lenny, if you were like, "Hey, Patrick, I like your shirt," and I just didn't like when people commented on my shirt, instead of getting pissed off, going to HR, or getting mad at you, what we would do is we'd say, "Hey, the right way at ProfitWell wall to handle that was be like, 'He didn't know, so I'm not going to bring it up,' or 'Hey, Lenny. 以下是我们采取的非常有效的措施。我认为，其中一个关键点在于，回归到你可能听过的基本反馈或建议——你无法让所有人都满意，所以你要明确自己的定位：你为谁服务，又不为谁服务？这需要在你的价值观中清晰界定，而价值观若非经由实际考验，往往流于空谈。因此，我们秉持"为长远利益优化"的原则。当以长远利益为先时，短期收益可能受损。（00:08:22）：此外，公司内不同类型的人在不同岗位上表现更优。我们采取的一个颇具争议的做法是，深入探讨行为准则，其中最重要的一条理念是"最善意的解读"。这并非我们首创的概念，但其核心理念在于，当出现冲突或对抗时，如何处理这种局面对我们至关重要。我们希望团队成员或应聘者能以最善意的角度看待这些冲突。（00:08:53）：举个例子，假设莱尼说"嘿，帕特里克，我喜欢你的衬衫"，而我不喜欢别人评论我的衬衫。面对这种情况，我们不会生气、找人事部门投诉或发脾气，而是会这样回应："在 ProfitWell，正确的处理方式应该是说‘他可能不知道，所以我不必提及此事’，或者‘莱尼，你可能不知道，但我确实不喜欢别人评论我的衬衫’。"
（00:09:14）：这看似微不足道，但当团队规模超过 20 人时，类似问题就会频发。我认为多数时候我们在把团队成员当孩子看待——让他们去找人事部门解决问题、制定各种政策，而最终你花大价钱请来聪明人才，却让他们陷入繁琐的政策纠纷中，而我们真正需要的是他们携手共进。

turns.en: That reminds me of there's this guy Douglas Atkin, who I worked with for a while who helped us craft the core values at Airbnb, and he made this point that your values need to be clear, exactly like you said, who doesn't fit, who doesn't belong. Because if it's everybody, it's worthless. Integrity, trust, everyone wants that and it fits into that, but it's only valuable if it's clear who's not a fit, exactly how you're saying it.
turns.zh: 这让我想起道格拉斯·阿特金（Douglas Atkin）这个人。我曾和他共事过一段时间，他帮助我们在Airbnb确立了核心价值观。他曾指出，你的价值观必须清晰明确——正如你所说，哪些人不符合，哪些人不属于这里。因为如果人人皆可，那就毫无价值。诚信、信任，每个人都渴望这些，但只有当你明确哪些人不合适时，这些价值观才有意义。正如你所说。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Well, we get this fear of that accommodation culture, again, where it starts even in the interview process, we're like, "Oh my god, we need these hires, we need these salespeople, we need these engineers." So we don't end up being upfront with these values and these trade-offs in the interview process. And then all of a sudden you spend a lot of time and a lot of money hiring someone who just doesn't fit. And I think that's really, really bad for them, it's really bad for you. And so that was the other thing is we would pull all of this forward into the interview process and talk about it and basically say like, "Hey, if this is not how you think, that's okay. We're not better than you, you're not better than us, it's just this is how we do things here." (00:11:42): And I think a lot of times we're scared to do that because we have that founder, that exact fear of, "Hey, we have to get this thing done and the only way to do that is to do X, Y or Z Z when in reality that's actually going to make your deadline go out further than actually focusing on alignment as much as humanly possible.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们对这种企业文化心存恐惧，这种恐惧甚至始于面试过程。我们会想：“天啊，我们需要这些新员工、销售人员、工程师。”所以在面试过程中，我们往往不直言这些价值观和取舍。结果突然花了大量时间和金钱，却招聘到不合适的人。我认为这对他们和我们都非常不利。因此，我们会把这些理念引入面试过程，坦诚沟通，比如说：“嘿，如果你不认同这些理念，没关系。我们不比你高明，你也不比我们优越，只是我们这里就是这么做事的。” （00:11:42）：但很多时候我们不敢这么做，因为我们有创始人心态，害怕“必须完成任务，而唯一的办法就是做X、Y或Z”，但实际上这样做只会让截止日期更遥远，而非尽可能地达成一致。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next topic, bootstrapping. I feel like you're probably in the bootstrap hall of fame. You built a company-
turns.zh: 下一个话题，白手起家。我觉得你可能是白手起家领域的名人堂成员。你创办了一家公司——

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Here we go. That's all I've ever wanted.
turns.zh: 开始吧。就说这些吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you're in there. So you tell me if I'm missing anything, but basically you bootstrapped a company, sold it for 200 million. I don't know if I've heard of anything like that. So what's your hot take? What are mistakes people make around bootstrapping?
turns.zh: 我觉得你确实属于这个行列。所以如果我有遗漏的地方，请告诉我，但基本上你白手起家创办了一家公司，以2亿美元的价格出售。我不知道是否有类似的案例。那你有什么独到见解？在白手起家方面人们常犯哪些错误？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: The basic idea is bootstrapping is for lifestyle businesses that want to cash flow. Funding is for companies trying to create a billion dollars in annual revenue. And that answer offends everybody. That answer offends the indie friends I have, they're going to be like, "Oh, what about Basecamp [inaudible 00:12:43], ProfitWell?" And I'll tell you, ProfitWell, this was a big mistake. Yes, it was a great exit, we sold for over $200 million, et cetera, but we probably, if we had taken money, we could have had a billion-dollar exit or we could have kept going. (00:12:56): And we should have taken money earlier in our life cycle. This was actually a big mistake because we got hooked on the efficiency and that was great, but we could have moved even quicker than we were. And hindsight is 20/20, and I'm obviously not crying over this, but it's one of those things that I think that you have to know who you are and you have to know what your goals are for a company. And our biggest thing was we wanted to build a big company and we were going after that, but we weren't doing the things in order to actually make that happen, which is i.e. getting funded. So yeah, that's my hot take and hopefully I offend everyone. But it's also just the end of the Twitter argument where it's like, "Yeah, it depends," but that's the thing to think about.
turns.zh: 基本思路是，白手起家适合想要现金流的个人生活方式型企业。融资则适合那些试图创造10亿美元年营收的公司。这种观点让所有人感到不满。那些独立创业的朋友会说：“哦，Basecamp（00:12:43）呢？ProfitWell呢？” 我告诉你，ProfitWell是个大错误。是的，那是一次不错的退出，我们以超过2亿美元的价格出售，但如果当时我们接受融资，或许能实现10亿美元的退出，或者继续发展下去。（00:12:56）：而且我们本应在早期就融资。这确实是个大错误，因为我们沉迷于效率感，这很棒，但本可以发展得更快。事后诸葛亮，我显然不为此感到遗憾，但这确实让我明白，你必须清楚自己是谁，明白公司的目标是什么。我们最大的错误是想建立一家大公司，并为此努力，但却没有采取实现这一目标的必要措施——即融资。所以是的，这就是我的独到见解，希望能得罪所有人。但这也正是Twitter辩论的终点，那就是“是的，这取决于情况”，但这才是值得深思的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting because usually you hear from the other end, someone that raised VC money is like, "I shouldn't have raised money, I should have bootstrapped this thing longer." It's cool to hear from the other side someone that did that like, "No, we maybe should have raised the VC money along the way."
turns.zh: 这一点很有意思，因为通常你会听到融资成功的创业者说，“我本不该融资的，应该多烧几年钱自力更生。” 而现在能听到融资反面案例的人说 “不，我们当初或许应该边做边融资”，这真的很酷。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Well, I think there's a lot of ideas that should not raise money. There's a lot of ideas that should just be great cash flowing and they can be large businesses. There's large businesses cash flowing tens of millions of dollars without funding. And I think it's just one of those things that you need your goals, your model, and ultimately your funding situation all to match. And I think a lot of folks, they go in the opposite direction where they're just like, "Oh, everything on TechCrunch, everything on Twitter is like, "Hey, I need to raise money, raise money, raise money." And they don't take a step back and go like, well that idea, it's just not a very good business to get money. And money is so plentiful even now still that it is, quote-unquote, "relatively easy" to raise money on, just not a great idea, and so that's obviously problematic.
turns.zh: 我认为很多项目本不该融资。很多业务只要现金流良好，本身就能发展成大公司。有些大公司在没有融资的情况下就能实现数千万美元的现金流。我觉得这事儿需要你的目标、商业模式和融资环境三者完美契合。很多创业者却反其道而行之，看到科技博客、推特上动不动就“要融资、要融资、要融资”，却从不反思自己的创意根本不适合融资。即便现在融资环境依然宽松，但有些项目融资并非明智之选，这显然是个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been thinking about writing a post on that exact topic, something like, "Your startup probably is not venture scale," because a lot of people think they could raise money and build a huge business. What's a heuristic that maybe tells a founder that they shouldn't raise money, it's never going to be a billion-dollar company?
turns.zh: 我正考虑写一篇关于这个话题的文章，标题可能是《你的初创公司很可能达不到风投级别》。因为很多人以为只要融资就能做大公司。那么有没有什么启发性标准，能让创始人意识到不该融资，因为这项业务注定成不了百亿美元级别的巨头？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I used to look at it 10 years ago you'd say, "Is this a company that can get to 100 million in annual revenue?" And now those numbers are all changed because IPOs are happening closer to 200, 250 million and the markets are all over the place depending on the day. I look at this as if you are going to be that large company, you need to get to a billion in revenue per year. It doesn't have to be overnight, it can be over 20 years, it's not something that has to happen quickly, but that's how I think about it. And if I don't feel like there's a clear path to that, it doesn't mean I don't raise money. It just means that I take a step back and really think about that particular idea because when you get on that treadmill, there's plenty of ideas that will sell for 400 million, 500 million. (00:15:38): But then if you're on the funding treadmill and you look at how much money that founder that exec team ends up getting at the end of it's like you might have been better just building a 50 million cash flowing business that you're getting more money from that and you still have the choice to sell it. (00:15:52): So that's how I think about it. It's a spectrum and it's on the margins there. It's not a fixed rule. But the other thing I also think about when I think about building my next company, we're going to be bootstrapped for, I don't know what... It's not a timeline, but I had imagined probably the first 18 to 24 months because I don't want to give up that equity for that funding on figuring out the idea. Obviously, I had an exit so I'm able to afford that and I'm in a position where I don't have to worry about my own livelihood. (00:16:22): But I think it's one of those things if you can bootstrap, even if you're going after a funded idea, if you can bootstrap for the initial ideation and maybe even through product market fit, which is not an easy thing to do, but that's the ideal time then to raise because then you're just going and you're going for the fences at that point.
turns.zh: 十年前我曾思考过这个问题，你可能会问：“这家公司能做到年营收1亿吗？” 如今这些数字已然变了样——IPO的估值动辄接近2亿、2.5亿，市场波动也因时而异。我认为，要想成为一家大型公司，年营收必须达到10亿。这并非一蹴而就的过程，可以用20年时间逐步实现，但这是我坚信的方向。如果看不到清晰的路径，我不会轻易融资，而是会退后一步，重新审视这个商业构想。毕竟，一旦踏上融资的跑步机，很容易被高估值冲昏头脑，追逐4亿、5亿的融资款项。但若深究融资后的结果，你会发现创始人及其团队最终获得的资金可能更少——还不如专注打造一个年营收5000万、现金流充足的业务，这样既能积累更多财富，又有退出选择权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that very concrete stat you shared and that's exactly how we think about it, that if you don't think you can get to a billion dollars in revenue a year eventually that it probably is not a venture-scale business. And I think that just boils down to how large is the market. If there's not enough people that are going to pay enough money to make this a billion dollar a year in revenue business, you probably shouldn't go down the VC treadmill.
turns.zh: 你分享的那个具体数据我很认同，这正是我们的核心观点：如果不相信最终能达到年营收10亿，那很可能这不是一家具备风险投资规模的企业。归根结底，关键在于市场规模。若没有足够的用户愿意为你的产品支付足够高的价格，年营收突破10亿的可能性微乎其微，那你就没必要走风险投资融资的路子。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: And I think when you think about that, it opens up this world of options for you as someone listening to this. And so think of it this way, you don't have to have the pressure to create a billion dollars in revenue If you can take a step back and be like, "Okay, I can create a $10-million business." You're listening to this and probably you're like, "I don't know." But if you were a director level somewhere at a corporate company or you're leading product somewhere, you can go create a $10-million business. It might not happen overnight, it might take 10 years, all these other things. But that's amazing. That's insane. (00:17:33): Think of 20, 30, 40, 50 years ago, you'd have to have a corner store and you'd have to work 18 hours a day to build that type of ability or that wealth to then hopefully retire when you're 65 and sell the business for 1X. Now you can build a software company that's doing a million a year, have an amazing life, reduce the number of hours if you want, or go all in, make it into a 10 or $100-million company over time. And I think that's amazing and we should celebrate that rather than if it's not a billion, you're failing. But we should just know our limits. I think that's the thing a lot of people fail out with funding.
turns.zh: 还有，我觉得当你思考这一点时，它为听众们打开了一个全新的选择世界。换个角度想，你不必承受创造十亿美元营收的压力。若能退一步想：“好吧，我能创办一家价值1000万美元的企业。”你听了这番话，可能心想：“我不确定能做到。” 但如果你是一家大公司的总监，或者负责产品开发的负责人，你完全可以创办一家价值1000万美元的企业。或许这并非一夜之间就能实现，可能需要十年时间，但这依然令人惊叹。这太不可思议了。（00:17:33） 回想二三十年前，你得开一家街边小店，每天工作18小时，才能积累起那样的财富，然后希望在65岁退休时能卖个一倍的价钱。如今，你可以创办一家年营收百万美元的软件公司，过上美好的生活。如果你愿意，还可以减少工作时长；或者全力以赴，逐步将公司发展成价值1000万甚至1亿美元的企业。我觉得这太棒了，我们应该为此庆贺，而不是把失败归咎于没能达到十亿美元营收。但我们也得认清自己的局限。我认为这正是许多人在融资时常犯的错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next topic, pricing. You are probably the most... okay, you're in the top 1% smartest, most experienced people on pricing. We could have done a whole podcast on pricing, maybe we will in the future, but as maybe one of 10 topics, what comes to mind as maybe the biggest mistake people make in pricing, biggest opportunity they miss, biggest hot take?
turns.zh: 接下来是定价话题。你很可能是……好吧，你是定价领域最聪明、最有经验的1%高手。我们本可以专门做一期关于定价的播客，或许未来会实现，但作为十个话题之一，你觉得人们在定价方面最常犯的错误、错失的最大机遇，以及最具争议的观点是什么？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: It's super boring, but the biggest hot take is you just have to do something once a quarter. That's it. I've been trying to teach about pricing for a decade now. I've done a lot of different approaches on this, and I think the easiest thing is, listen, you have three growth levers. You have acquiring customers, monetizing them, and retaining them. You're spending a lot of time and money on acquisition. You're spending some time and money on retention. You're probably do nothing on pricing and monetization and it's because you think it's this nebulous thing and there are some nebulous aspects to it. (00:19:06): But to make it super concrete, it is the revenue per customer. Look at that number, that one KPI, and you want that number going up and to the right, it's obviously going to go to the right over time, but you want it to going up over time every single quarter, not as high as your sales volume or your lead volume or your revenue maybe. But you want that number gradually going up and just do one thing per quarter. The least sexy thing when it comes to pricing is have a pricing committee. If it's a two-person company, it's you and your co-founder. If it's a 100,000-person company, it might be 30 people, but really it's only eight people central to that particular product. (00:19:42): And then just realize there's a lot of things that influence that revenue per customer. There's the actual price, your packaging, your add-on strategy, your discount strategy, your price localization, freemium. There's a whole host of different things there, but just find one thing you're going to do every three months, put a calendar invite, let it renew every three months. You're going to snooze it a couple of times, I get it, I've seen this many, many times before. But just do something, even if it's super small. I guarantee you it's just like any other thing you measure, as soon as you start measuring and caring about it, you're going to start to do some stuff, some of it is going to go poorly, some of it is going to go great. Then you're going to do more stuff, and then just over time, all of a sudden that number's going to go up into the right. But just do something. That's the basic idea.
turns.zh:
这听起来很无聊，但最重要的观点是，你只需每季度做一件事。就是这样。我研究定价策略已经十年了，尝试过各种方法。我认为最简单的方法是，听着，企业有三个增长杠杆：获取客户、变现客户、留住客户。你在获取客户上投入大量时间和金钱，在留住客户上也花了些心思，但在定价和变现方面可能毫无建树，因为你觉得这件事太模糊，确实存在一些不确定性。

（00:19:06）但要具体化一点，就是客户单价。看看这个关键绩效指标（KPI），你希望这个数字向上和向右增长。虽然随着时间推移它自然会上升，但你希望每个季度都逐季递增，虽然可能比不上销售额、潜在客户数量或总收入的增长，但至少要确保这个数字稳步攀升。每个季度只需做一件事。

在定价方面，成立定价委员会是最没用的做法。两人的公司可能只有你和联合创始人，10万人的公司可能有30人，但核心团队通常只有8人。（00:19:42）要记住，影响客户单价的因素有很多：实际价格、产品包装、附加服务策略、折扣策略、价格本土化策略、免费增值模式等。总之，每季度只需专注一件事。设置日历提醒，每三个月重复一次。你可能会多次拖延提醒，我理解这种心理，我见过太多类似情况。但只要行动起来，哪怕微不足道的改进，都会带来积极反馈。只要持续关注数据，自然会找到改进方向，过程可能曲折，但最终结果必然显著。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the simplicity of that. If I think about the pie chart of the things you will do and may change, you mentioned a few. One is raise prices. One may be lower prices. One's probably change your pricing model. There's a couple more. I guess, in your experience, where have you found the biggest opportunities end up being maybe early in the early phase of a startup in that pie chart?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种简单直白的观点。回想你提到的可能需要调整的领域，比如提价、降价、调整定价模式等。我想根据你的经验，创业初期在定价方面最容易找到突破口的阶段在哪里？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: The number one thing to figure out when you're thinking about the different pricing pieces, pound for pound, it's the pricing metric or the value metric. That's how you charge per user, per thousand visits, per thousand what's its, whatever it is. Consumer companies, it's a little bit harder. Physical good products, it's really hard obviously because you have that physical good, the physics you can't get over. But the reason this is so powerful is because if you get everything else in your pricing wrong or not great, but you get that right, you tend to be okay when it comes to monetization. (00:21:21): And the reason is because, first, from an acquisition standpoint like acquiring customers, you end up making sure that you get Disney coming into your product, they're paying Disney prices, and then you get Johnny or Jane's startup coming in and they're paying Johnny and Jane prices. You don't want them paying the same thing because obviously the value's different, even if they're consuming almost the same amount. So this allows you to figure that line out. (00:21:44): And then what's really beautiful about it is churn tends to be about 20 to 25% lower because people will downgrade, but they're using... you don't get this like, "I'm paying for so much and end up not using a lot of it." It's like, "Oh, I'm using eight seats this month, I'm going to downgrade," or it's just automatic. And then your expansion revenue's typically double when you're using a particular value metric because instead of me having to resell you and being like, "Hey, Lenny, there's this really cool feature in this upper tier, do you want this?" And you're like, "I already use the product, I don't really want this." Instead, I just go, "Hey, Lenny, congratulations. You now have 100 videos in your account. That's awesome. You guys must be growing. I'm just going to bump you up to the 100-video plan. Let me know if you have any questions." It's just a very, very implicit way to get expansion revenue. So that's the thing pound for pound that's the best. (00:22:30): And then I would say if you have a lot of politics internally, which everyone does with pricing because it sits in the center of so many different teams, I would actually start with a price increase. You should be increasing your overall price once per year if you're building. If you're not building and your support sucks and your NPS is low, then don't worry about it. But if your NPS is over 20, which is not a very high NPS, you should raise your prices once per year. The reason I suggest that is because it gets all of the BS and all the politics on the mat. You're going to have to collect some data, you're going to have to prove it to sales, you're going to have to make sure you have the enablement, you're going to have to make sure your messaging is... (00:23:06): But it's a tight enough non-nebulous thing that you're doing versus a value metric where you can have a bunch of debates about this metric or that metric, and should you give 10 away versus 100 away. It's a good way to rip the bandaid off. And most companies don't change their actual number that they're charging once per every three years. So if you haven't done it for three years, you're overdue for it. So it's a good one to kind of rip the bandaid off.
turns.zh: 考虑不同定价策略时，最关键的是要明确一个核心问题：无论是按用户收费、千次访问收费，还是其他任何定价方式，最终都要回归到一个核心指标——定价或价值衡量标准。消费类产品在这方面相对容易，但实体商品就困难得多，因为物理属性限制难以突破。但这套逻辑之所以有效，是因为如果其他定价环节出错或不完善，但定价策略正确，变现效果往往不会太差。（00:21:21）：首先从获取客户的角度看，消费者进入产品后，他们支付的费用差异巨大，比如迪士尼用户和普通初创公司用户的定价标准完全不同。不能让他们支付相同的费用，因为即使消费量相近，价值也存在天壤之别。这就需要精准划分用户层级。（00:21:44）：更妙的是，客户流失率通常能降低20%至25%，因为用户会根据实际使用情况降级服务，而非因价格不合理而产生不满。例如用户本月使用了8个席位，就会主动降级，而不是被动接受升级提议。（00:22:30）：最有效的定价策略是采用价值衡量标准。无需反复推销升级服务，直接告知用户：“恭喜你，账户已有100个视频，说明业务发展迅速。我们将为你升级至100个视频套餐，如有疑问随时联系。”这是一种隐性变现方式。（00:23:06）：若公司内部对定价存在诸多政治博弈（毕竟定价涉及多个团队），可以先从提价开始。若产品尚在开发阶段，建议每年调价一次；若支持服务不达标、NPS低于20%，则暂缓涨价。核心在于通过数据验证、销售培训和信息传递，确保涨价合理。与争论各种指标相比，价值定价更直观易懂。三年不调价的公司无异于拖延改革，趁早行动吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this episode already pound for pound I think is up there. This is amazing. I'm excited to get to the next topic, but first I'll plug. You wrote a guest post in my newsletter about pricing and we'll link to that in the show notes, and that goes deeper into this value metric and how to think about pricing. So check that out. (00:23:46): Next topic, retention. So when I think Patrick Campbell, I think pricing and retention. So again, this could be its own podcast episode, but let's just pick one thing to talk about. What are the biggest mistakes people make, retention opportunities, or just hot take?
turns.zh: 到目前为止，我觉得这一集已经相当精彩了。这太棒了。我很期待接下来要讨论的主题，但首先我要宣传一下。你在我的新闻通讯中写了一篇关于定价的客座文章，我们会在节目笔记中附上链接，那篇文章会更深入地探讨这个价值指标以及如何思考定价策略。所以大家可以去看看。（00:23:46）接下来是留存率话题。一提到帕特里克·坎贝尔，我的脑海中首先浮现的就是定价和留存率。不过这本身也可以单独做一期播客，但这次我们就选一个点来聊聊。大家在留存率方面最常犯的错误有哪些？有哪些提升留存率的机会？或者你们有什么独到的见解？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: The reason I started writing about retention and publishing data on it is because I didn't want to be the pricing guy. I was trying to basically differentiate myself and then I was trying to be the SaaS guy, but that's too broad. But anyway, so retention, the hottest of hottest takes, and this is the one to offend 90% of the list... no, it's not going to offend, but this is a product podcast, that's how I think about it. Product homies. You fail at realizing most of the time that there are two types of retention. There is strategic retention and then there's tactical retention. (00:24:38): Strategic retention is all the stuff that you as a great product leader, a great product team are doing. Your ICPs, your time to value, road mapping, the right features, figuring out your mission metric, agonizing over every little thing, all the paper cuts of being a great product leader. But because you're so focused and so biased towards that, you miss out typically on this thing we call tactical retention, and these are things like payment failures, term optimization, cancellation flows, offboarding, et cetera. And if you're past product market fit this area, this tactical retention, it's typically about 25 to 40% of your churn problem, which is a significant amount, but you don't really look at it because again, you're like, "I've got to go focus on features, I've got to do this, and I'm going to go be this great product leader." (00:25:26): And so because product is so entrenched in that thinking that that problem can be solved with two months of work, it's not that much work putting in, basically, a marketing funnel when people's credit cards fail. Not that hard, not rocket science. Doing offboarding, being really smart with offboarding. And one little tidbit. I looked at two million cancellation flows. We built some products for this, that's why I have this data, just to be clear. But looked at two million cancellation flows and we found you have about 18 to 30 seconds when someone hits that cancel button, we found you should ask two questions. One, "Why are you leaving?" Multiple choice. Don't do the free response. You get one out of 100 great responses, and the 99 are not great. (00:26:08): And then the other question we found works really, really well is, "What did you like about the product?" And the reason that works so effectively is because that person's on a freight train to basically cancel. They're like, "I'm already done. Oh yeah, this is why I'm leaving." The minute you ask them what they like, you're basically tapping into this nostalgia effect and you're stopping that freight train. And then when I have that information, it's great for a product team, it's great to figure out, "What's working, what's not? What should we do more of? Was this a good customer?" (00:26:34): But then based on their engagement data, their plan, whatever, all their firmographics about them plus their answers, then I can offer up a salvage offer or a pause plan or a maintenance plan or these types of things. But all this type of stuff, this is really, really powerful. And I always suggest finance teams should just take this on because product teams are always going to be thinking so much more on the future rather than fixing this right now. But that's the hottest take I've got for retention.
turns.zh: 我之所以开始研究用户留存并发布相关数据，是因为我不想只做定价专家。我曾试图通过差异化定位来提升自己的价值，但SaaS领域太过宽泛了。不过说回来，留存问题确实是当前最热门的话题——但它也会得罪90%的听众……不，应该说这只是个产品播客，我是这么看的。各位产品同行们，你们大多忽视了一个关键点：留存问题分为两类——战略性留存和战术性留存。（00:24:38）战略性留存指的是优秀的产品领导者和团队所做的工作，比如客户画像、价值实现时间、路线图规划、核心功能设计、使命指标制定等，这些都是产品经理日常钻研的细节。但由于过于专注战略层面，你们往往忽视了战术层面的留存问题——比如支付失败处理、续费优化、取消流程、离职流程等。当产品市场验证成功后，这些战术性问题往往占据客户流失的25%至40%，这是一个不容忽视的比例。但你们总会说：“我得专注功能开发，完成这个项目，成为伟大的产品领袖。”（00:25:26）产品团队深陷“两个月就能解决问题”的思维误区，殊不知处理客户信用卡支付失败时的营销漏斗并不复杂。比如建立离职流程时，只要在用户点击取消按钮的18到30秒内提出两个问题：第一，“你为什么离开？”采用多选题形式，避免开放式回答（100个回复中只有一个优质，其余皆不可用）。第二，“你喜欢这款产品的哪些方面？”这种策略能有效阻止用户流失，因为用户此时正处于离开的冲动阶段，回答问题能激活他们的怀旧情结。结合用户互动数据、行为特征及反馈结果，产品团队就能制定挽回策略、暂停计划或维护方案。这些方法的价值远超想象。我始终建议财务团队主导此类工作，毕竟产品团队往往更关注未来，却忽视了当下问题的解决。但这确实是关于留存问题最深刻的见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great, awesome take. And I want to plug ProfitWell right here, actually. I know you guys offer a product that does this and I've used it. So I don't know if that's still true, I know after an acquisition, things change. So I use ProfitWell for my newsletters. I just plug it into my Stripe account and it's the most amazing free product because it just tells me everything I want to know. And then it's got this cool feature, you just turn it on and it does these things for you like it tells people, "Your credit card is about to expire." Hey, this card failed, you should try putting in a new card." So that's a cool reason to check out ProfitWell.
turns.zh: 太棒了，真是个超赞的观点！说真的，我特别想推荐一下 ProfitWell。我知道你们有相关产品，我自己也用过。虽说收购后情况可能会有变，但我现在还是用它来管理我的新闻通讯。只需把它接入 Stripe 账户，就能获取所有关键信息。这款产品简直免费得令人惊叹，它能自动完成所有繁琐任务，比如提醒用户信用卡即将到期、提示卡片失效需要更新信息等。这就是推荐 ProfitWell 的绝佳理由。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Thanks, man. I appreciate that. And it's actually cool because I think for us, because the fact that product teams don't really think about this stuff, we stumbled into this whole thesis that could be a whole episode, which is all the product features are done for you. So what I mean by that is, you noticed this, but when you log in and set this up, you're not writing emails, you're not setting up the flows. And the reason is because we have all this data from $30 billion in ARR flowing through our metrics product that we can study and understand what works and what doesn't. (00:28:02): And that kind of stumbling that is useful for folks is what we discovered is this anti-active usage type product, it retains itself at a really, really high rate because people are just getting the value and they don't have to use it. And so what we found is a little bonus thing on retention. When we look at churn rates across different types of products, those products that are workflow products you use every single day or mostly every single day, or those products you don't have to log into but you still get the value, that's where the lowest churn rates are, the highest retention. Anything in the middle, it's like death. And this is why ProfitWell metrics ended up being free because we were just like, "It's terrible to build a metrics and analytics product. It's so hard because people just don't appreciate how much work goes into it, therefore they don't retain at a high rate, they're not willing to pay that much," et cetera.
turns.zh: 多谢提醒，兄弟。这真的很棒，因为我们产品团队之前根本没考虑过这些细节。结果我们偶然发现了一个可以写成整期播客的核心理念——让产品功能自动化。具体来说，用户无需手动操作邮件设置或流程配置，因为我们有价值 300 亿美元 ARR（年度经常性收入）的数据流入指标产品，通过分析能清楚哪些功能有效，哪些无效。（00:28:02）这种无需主动使用的反向自动化产品，用户留存率极高，因为他们能直接获取价值而无需额外操作。对比之下，其他类型的产品（比如日用型或无需登录即可享受价值的产品）流失率最低，留存率最高。处于中间状态的产品则容易失败。这就是 ProfitWell 指标产品免费开放的根本原因——我们当时想：“打造分析产品太难了，用户根本不明白其中的开发投入，所以留存率低，用户不愿付费。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that alone is a really interesting story, and I don't know if we should get too deep, but just to highlight what you just said, so many startups build an analytics product that it's just a better way to measure and track all the stuff that's going on. And what you've found is you won't make money doing that, people don't want to pay for a SaaS analytics tool.
turns.zh: 单说这点就很有意思，虽然不必深挖，但还是想强调你刚才提到的观点。太多初创公司打造分析产品，试图更高效地衡量和追踪业务数据。但你们发现这条路走不通，用户不愿为 SaaS 分析工具付费。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: You have two options. You go up market and you pretty much become a data product with a UI or you go super niche. And even super niche, it's super hard and it's just because, I don't know, everyone's trying to kill a spreadsheet, and it's like, "You're not going to kill a spreadsheet." All real analysts will do everything in a spreadsheet. So for us it was we want to give you a clean UI and then we want to help you get this data into spreadsheets or email or whatever you're using for your databases, things like that.
turns.zh: 有两种选择：要么向高端市场进军，打造带有 UI 的数据产品；要么走极端垂直路线。但即便走垂直路线也异常艰难，因为人们都在试图取代电子表格，但事实是，真正的分析师仍会用电子表格完成所有工作。对我们来说，目标是提供简洁的 UI，帮助用户将数据整合到电子表格、邮件或数据库等工具中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I don't want to make this an ad for ProfitWell, but it's like founders come to me with pitches of, "Hey, we've built this sweet analytics." So I'm like, "Just look up what ProfitWell is giving away for free, that's going to be a high bar to exceed."
turns.zh: 是啊，我不想把这变成 ProfitWell 的广告，但很多创业者来找我推销时都会说：“我们开发了超棒的分析工具。”我就会说：“去看看 ProfitWell 免费提供的功能吧，这标准实在太高了。”

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. We were going to try to sell it. We were trying to sell it in the beginning, but what ended up happening is we ran into all this, that's why we didn't.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。我们本来打算试着把它卖掉的。一开始我们确实想卖掉它，但后来遇到了一堆麻烦，所以就没卖成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, back on track. Topic number five, shipping. What have you learned about shipping? What are mistakes people make when trying to ship faster, ship more efficiently?
turns.zh: 好的，回到正题。第五个话题，运输。关于运输，你们有什么心得？在试图加快运输速度、提高运输效率时，人们常会犯哪些错误？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah. The bratty thing here is that real professional ship. At the end of the day, real... I don't care what if you're a marketer or product person, engineer, ops person, people ops, real professional ship, and they ship it a pretty high frequency for whatever they're doing. And so the thing that we thought a lot about is, in my opinion, your tempo framework, and I'll explain a little bit more of what that means in a second, is more important than your org design. And so if you've ever had a team that seems really, really smart, but they're always planning or they don't really ship a lot, or you've had trouble where everyone gets it at the leadership level, but then the team below them and below them seems to be kind of going in a different direction, you probably don't have enough alignment and you don't have enough alignment on what good looks like in terms of tempo. (00:30:56): And so the way we looked at this was we have to establish mission metric and guiding principles at the top so, what do we do? How are we measuring it? And how we're going to get there? So for us was we automate subscription growth. Our mission metric was the amount of revenue that was on ProfitWell because that was good from acquisition, but it also meant we were doing our jobs. Then how we're going to get there. We want to be the most helpful brand in SaaS. And then we also we're going to do it for you, this whole thing that I just talked about. (00:31:25): Then what we did is we established that at the leadership level, every org leader, so marketing, sales, et cetera, they need a framework that fits into that overall. So marketing at ProfitWell was this whole inbound media, so lots of podcast, video series, et cetera. And the most important part of that was they needed to determine what good looked like in terms of shipping. So if we're like, "Hey, we're doing sales," blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, or marketing in this case, "this many episodes per month, it's this many product launches per month, this many big product launches per quarter," whatever it is. (00:31:57): And then your leadership is basically a conversation of, "Great, that's what good looks like, we agree. How do we close that gap?" And then all of those conversations are like, "Okay, you only shipped one thing per quarter, we want to do one per month. Why?" (00:32:10): "Well, I don't have enough resources." (00:32:12): We solve that problem or we figure out how to get the more resources, then they're not doing it again. "Okay, why?" (00:32:17): "Well, there's this problem." (00:32:18): And then all of a sudden you start to create this very high output team across the board, and you also have this alignment so you don't wake up nine months into someone being at your company and being like, "Well, I think Tim sucks." (00:32:30): And it's like, "Well, why did you just all of a sudden wake up and think Tim sucks." (00:32:34): "Well, he's not shipping blah, blah, blah, blah." (00:32:35): "Well, it's probably an org problem rather than a Tim problem," because again, you vetted Tim. Tim was at this other company and apparently was a really great rockstar. So what's the difference here? You screwed up the hiring? Well, maybe because that is really, really hard, but most of the time you just haven't set an expectation of what good looks like in terms of tempo, and then you haven't had that constant conversation to make sure that Tim has what he needs in order to ship.
turns.zh: 是啊。这里最烦人的地方在于真正的专业协作。说到底，真正的……我不在乎你是市场营销人员、产品经理、工程师、运营人员，还是人力资源专员，但真正专业的协作意味着他们能以相当高的频率交付成果。关于这点，我们思考了很多，我认为你的节奏框架比组织设计更重要。（00:30:56）：所以如果你曾遇到过这样情况——团队看似非常聪明，但他们总是在规划，却很少真正交付成果；或者你遇到过领导层达成共识，但下级团队却朝着不同方向发展——那很可能是因为你们在节奏标准上缺乏一致性。（00:31:25）：我们的做法是，在领导层面确立使命指标和指导原则。比如，我们如何衡量成功？如何达成目标？对我们来说，目标是实现订阅增长。我们的使命指标是ProfitWell平台上的收入数额，因为这既能体现获客效果，也是我们是否在履行职责的证明。然后是如何达成目标。我们要成为SaaS领域最有价值的品牌。接着，我们要为此付出努力——就像我刚才提到的。（00:31:57）：接下来，我们在领导层面建立了一个统一框架，让每个部门（市场营销、销售等）都遵循这个大框架。以ProfitWell的市场营销为例，我们推出了全方位的入站媒体策略，比如播客、视频系列等。最重要的是，他们需要明确交付成果的标准。比如，销售团队可能会说：“我们每月要发布多少新功能，每季度要推出多少重大产品发布。”（00:32:10）：“嗯，但我们没有足够的资源。”（00:32:12）：我们要解决这个问题，或者想办法获取更多资源，然后他们才能继续推进。（00:32:17）：“好吧，是因为这个问题。”（00:32:18）：突然间，你就能打造一支高产出的团队，而且上下级之间也达成了一致。比如，九个月后新员工加入公司却说：“我觉得Tim太烂了。” （00:32:30）：“等等，你为什么突然觉得Tim不行了？” （00:32:34）：“因为他交付成果太慢了。” （00:32:35）：“那很可能是组织的问题，而不是Tim的问题。”因为毕竟你之前验证过Tim的能力。他在前公司可是个明星员工。那么差别在哪里？是招聘环节出了问题吗？或许是因为这确实很难，但更多时候只是因为你没有设定清晰的节奏标准，也没有持续沟通，确保Tim获得完成任务所需的支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was a big learning, I guess, in doing that? Is that just something you built up over time of we need to create this tempo at ProfitWell?
turns.zh: 嗯，我想在做这件事时最大的收获是什么？是需要逐步建立这种节奏感，还是说在 ProfitWell 公司我们天生就具备这种节奏感？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah. Complete misalignment if you don't call it out on what good looks like, just complete misalignment. Like so-and-so is going and building, they think one product launch per quarter. Or I'm sitting there and I'm like, "Well, we should have a medium one per month and then we should have a big one per quarter." Complete misalignment. And if you don't have a way to talk about that, some sort of nexus to have that conversation, you end up not having it, and then you end up creating this friction and resentment on both sides because everyone thinks, again, "Tim isn't doing well." And it's like, "That's not what's happening. It's just the expectations aren't set." (00:33:40): And then what was really cool is that you start to find out that the why they aren't hitting what good looks like is all solvable, and most of the time it's this team isn't talking to this team. "Oh, great. Well, marketing wants to do these launches, product isn't providing them stuff. All right, let's get these two people together, have this conversation because we didn't have product marketing or official product marketing." They have this conversation and then all of a sudden it's like, "All right, Neil, you need to provide one thing a month. There's so much stuff we've built, a lot of it we haven't announced, you just need to provide one thing a month. Marketing will worry about how to position it in a way that isn't too far, isn't overselling it, but also gets us something per month, and you can approve that positioning." And then all of a sudden you start getting this tempo going, which obviously is the goal.
turns.zh:
对。如果你不明确好产品的标准定义，那就会产生严重的信息不对称。比如某个人在开发产品时，他们可能认为每个季度只需发布一款产品。而我会觉得，每个月应该有一个中等规模的产品发布，每季度再推出一个大版本。这就是严重的信息不对称。如果你没有一个沟通机制来明确这些标准，最终就会产生摩擦和不满情绪，因为每个人都会觉得“蒂姆做得不好”。但实际上问题不在于他个人，而在于沟通不畅。
（00:33:40）最妙的是，当你发现问题根源后，很多矛盾其实都可以解决。很多时候，问题在于团队之间缺乏沟通。比如，市场部想尽快发布产品，但产品部门却没有提供足够的素材。这时候你就需要把双方召集起来，沟通协作。通过这样的对话，最终达成共识：“尼尔，你每月需要提供一份产品素材。我们已经积累了大量未发布的素材，你只需每月提供一份即可。市场部会负责包装产品，确保宣传既不过分夸大又能吸引用户，同时每月都能为我们带来收益，你只需批准最终的定位方案。”这样一来，节奏感就自然而然地形成了，这正是我们的最终目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me, David Sacks has this awesome post called The Cadence around how marketing and product and sales should operate and create this kind of cadence. So being aligned but also offset schedule, which will link to them in the show notes if you haven't seen it.
turns.zh: 这让我想起大卫·萨克斯（David Sacks）的一篇精彩文章《节奏感》，里面详细阐述了市场、产品和销售团队如何协同工作，形成这种节奏感。如果你没读过这篇文章，我会在节目笔记中附上链接。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah, that's great.
turns.zh: 是的，这确实很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next topic. First principles thinking. As a renaissance man of a brain, I feel like you've spent a lot of time thinking about from first principles and in our conversations you always have really interesting approaches to things. What have you learned about actually implementing first principle thinking, which people are always talking about. How do I [inaudible 00:35:00] first principle?
turns.zh: 接下来是首要原则思维。作为一个多面手，我觉得你花了大量时间从首要原则出发进行思考。在我们的交流中，你总能提出非常有趣的见解。对于人们常提到的首要原则思维，你有什么实际应用方面的体会？如何将首要原则应用到实践中呢？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah, people always talk about it. And there are no good courses that I have found on first principles thinking. There are good blog posts, but the good blog posts kind of explain what it is, and then that's it. It's like, "This is what it is, and here's an example." And most of them quote Elon Musk about rockets and breaking down the different parts. So what I kind of found is there's the five whys, which I think someone's talked before or at least I've read it in the newsletter before, which is just you keep asking why. Kind of, "Well, this is this way." (00:35:36): "Well, why is that?" (00:35:36): "Well, this is this way." (00:35:37): "Why is that?" (00:35:38): I found the model that people who aren't great at first principal thinking or aren't great at talking about it that kind of helps them unlock is this thing called problem, cause, solution. So I learned this in debate in college and high school, and it basically is you have a problem that you're trying to solve. Well, you can't actually solve a problem. So if we talk about world hunger, you can't just solve world hunger because it's kind of the symptom, it's this problem that exists. (00:36:06): Well then I want to break down what are all the causes of world hunger? And it's a little more brainstormy when you have these conversations with folks, especially again when they struggle with this. And all of a sudden I could list out all the causes, irrigation crisis, aid not getting to where it needs to be, famines, drought, et cetera. And then what I can do is I can rank those causes in terms of magnitude. So if we're trying to solve world hunger, and for some reason we discovered irrigation was the biggest problem, if we solved irrigation, everything would be great, well then I'm going to align my solutions to all of those different causes. And you get this nice alignment between, well, I can solve a cause, and if I solve the cause that's big enough and proper enough, I'm going to eventually solve the actual problem or mitigate the problem, I should say. (00:36:50): So that's the framework that I found really, really useful. And also, it's great for using for presentations, it's great for a mission, it's great for all of these different things because it's a little bit more actionable than just the five whys, which is more of a way to have a conversation.
turns.zh: 是啊，大家老是谈论这个话题。但我还没找到关于第一性原理思维的优质课程。倒是有一些不错的博客文章，但它们大多只是解释了这个概念，然后就结束了。比如，“这就是第一性原理思维”之类的，接着举个例子。大多数文章还引用埃隆·马斯克关于火箭拆解的例子。所以我发现了一个叫“五个为什么”的方法，我觉得之前有人提过，或者至少我在某个时事通讯里读到过，就是不断追问“为什么”。比如，“嗯，这样做的原因是……”（00:35:36）：“那为什么呢？”（00:35:36）：“嗯，这样做的原因是……”（00:35:37）：“为什么呢？”（00:35:38）。我发现对于那些不擅长第一性原理思维或不善于谈论它的人来说，一个能帮助他们打开思路的模型叫“问题、原因、解决方案”。我在大学和高中辩论时就学过这个模型。基本上，当你试图解决一个问题时，实际上你并不能直接解决问题。比如谈论世界饥饿问题，你不能直接解决这个问题，因为它只是一个症状，是一个存在的根本问题。（00:36:06）那接下来你要拆解导致世界饥饿的所有原因是什么？当你和别人讨论这个问题时，特别是当他们对此感到困惑时，就会有更多的头脑风暴。突然之间，我能列出所有原因：灌溉危机、援助物资无法送达、饥荒、干旱等等。然后我可以根据这些原因的重要性进行排序。比如，如果我们试图解决世界饥饿问题，而发现灌溉是最大的问题，那么只要解决了灌溉问题，一切都会迎刃而解。接下来，我会将我的解决方案与所有这些不同原因相结合。这样就能形成一个很好的逻辑关系，即我可以解决一个原因，如果我解决了足够重要、恰当的那个原因，最终就能解决实际问题或减轻问题的影响。（00:36:50）所以这就是我发现非常非常有用的框架。它也非常适合用于演示、制定使命宣言，以及其他各种场景，因为它比“五个为什么”更具可操作性，而“五个为什么”更多的是一种对话方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the way you operationalize this, say problem, cause, solution. You're saying on strategy templates, you write out, "Here's the problem we're trying to solve, here's the source of the issue, and then here's how we're approaching it." Can you talk a bit more about how you implement this at your company and the people you work with?
turns.zh: 那么，你如何将这个框架付诸实践呢？比如问题、原因、解决方案。你说在战略模板中，你会写下：“这里是我们试图解决的问题，这里是问题的根源，然后是我们的解决方法。”你能否详细谈谈如何在你的公司和与同事一起应用这个框架？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah, totally. So I'll say big, medium and small things, and I'll try to be really quick. So big things it's like, "What are we facing?" (00:37:30): "Oh, we're going to try to charge for this metrics product. Now there's a bunch of competitors. The customers don't really care about it." (00:37:37): So we have this problem and the problem is growth. How do we grow a product like this? How do we grow our company? And what's really interesting about a big problem or a nebulous problem like that is you end up having a lot of conversations about the problem, which I think is more useful sometimes about, "Well, what are we actually trying to do? Let's get alignment as much as possible." And then it's like, "Okay. Well, what are the causes of our growth problem?" (00:38:00): "Well, people aren't willing to pay for metrics. Getting accuracy is really, really hard. Actually, the market stance," all these other things. (00:38:08): "Well, what are some of the solutions?" (00:38:10): "Well, we could do this, could do this, could do this." (00:38:12): And normally what ends up happening is the solution ends up being kind of an approach. So our approach that mitigated or solved for some of these causes and mitigate the problem was freemium, and then these paid products that were all pay-for-performance because with pay-for-performance, you could charge a significant amount more in a market that only has 100,000 logos, which is a really small market. And so that kind of an example there. (00:38:37): Medium and small, let's talk about a support ticket. This person's pissed off. They're coming in, they're pissed off. What are the causes? Well, there's a lot of different causes that were probably like, "Oh, we didn't get back to them in time, and then we gave a crappy solution, we gave this..." It just kind of allows us to look at the problem. And so it's more of a way of thinking on that level. And it's not happening. We're not going to have an hour-long conversation about a support ticket. But the support folks that I've talked to about this, they go, "Okay, cool. Why is he upset?" (00:39:06): "Well, we didn't get the answer in time." (00:39:08): Okay, my first line is going to be, "I understand we didn't get you an answer quick enough. Apologies for that." It just allows them to have a little bit of an extra second to think through things and move forward with that.
turns.zh:
是的，完全正确。所以我会说一些大问题和小问题，并且尽量说得简洁明了。大问题比如，“我们面临什么挑战？”（00:37:30）：“哦，我们打算对这个度量产品收费。现在竞争对手太多了，用户对此并不感兴趣。”（00:37:37）  
我们面临的难题是增长问题。如何让产品实现增长？如何推动公司发展？面对这种大而模糊的问题，最有价值的做法是反复探讨问题核心，比如“我们到底想做什么？尽可能达成共识。”接着再追问：“增长问题的根源是什么？” （00:38:00）：“用户不愿为度量付费。提高准确性极其困难。市场定位等诸多因素影响。” （00:38:08）：“那有哪些解决方案呢？” （00:38:10）：“可以这么做、可以那么做。” （00:38:12）  
最终的解决方案往往是一种策略。我们的策略是通过免费增值模式来缓解或解决这些问题，随后推出按效果付费的付费产品。在仅有10万个标识的微型市场中，按效果付费模式能收取更高的费用。这就是一个典型案例。  

接下来是小而具体的问题，比如处理客户支持工单。用户生气了，抱怨服务差。根源可能在于回复不及时、解决方案质量低下。这种思维方式能帮助我们剖析问题。虽然我们不会为一个支持工单展开长篇大论，但与我交流过的支持团队会说：“好的，我需要了解用户为何不满。” （00:39:06）：“因为回复不及时，很抱歉。” （00:39:08）  
我的首句话会是：“理解你们回复不及时，很抱歉。” 这能让对方多一秒思考时间，更高效地推进解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I love that big example and a small example.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个例子。大问题和小问题的对比很到位。
