turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Next topic, customer research. I feel like you have a pretty interesting perspective on custom research, so let's go into it.
turns.zh: 好的。下一个主题是客户研究。我觉得你对客户研究的看法相当有趣，所以我们来深入探讨一下。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I think I have the 85-year-old curmudgeonly man perspective on customer research. So here's the thing. Everything in your business, it does not matter what type of business you have, everything is used to drive someone to a point of conversion or justify the product or the price that you're offering up. That customer is a human being you're driving to that point of conversion and it's your job to understand how they perceive you, how they perceive their problem, how they perceive the world around them, around your products. (00:41:00): We all know this on a philosophical level, but here are some fun facts. So one, only one in five companies have buyer personas or ICPs, only one in five. So we talk about this all the time, we retweet the articles, we give the advice, so many of us give the advice. But then we look at our own companies, only one in five have some sort of segmentation ICPs. And then only one out of 10 companies actually do customer research or development on a quarterly basis. This should be a continuous thing, it should be a monthly, weekly type thing. Not saying you're sending up surveys or having all these conversations on a weekly basis, but only one out of 10 are doing quarterly. So that means the number they're doing monthly is even smaller than that. And I just think that's insane. (00:41:44): And when we look at all data, and we have a lot of data on this, and this is something where I've been talking about customer development for a long time. Everything is better. Everything is better. NPS is higher for organizations that have customer development functions or even just ICPs or buyer personas, depending on what framework you're using. Willingness to pay is typically higher. The funnel is more efficient. LTV to CAC is normally much, much higher. All those growth numbers, you're typically growing in a much higher rate, like a 15, 20%, not a small delta, 15-20% higher rate. Retention's better. All these things are better. (00:42:21): And the thing that, I think, 20 years ago or 10 years ago you didn't have to do customer development because, and this is where Keith [inaudible 00:42:30] is just like customer research is dumb or whatever his famous quote is, but you didn't have to do it because there just wasn't a lot of stuff out there and we all were riding the wave of the internet. But now the market's harder and harder. So what are you going to do? Are you just going to keep throwing stuff up against the wall or are you going to actually do the stuff that all of us talk about doing and actually do the research? And the research is hard. It's never going to be 100% accurate because you're going to have to use your judgment, but that's your job. (00:42:54): And so that's more of a rant, I guess, than a hot take. But I also think this is one of those things that AI starts solving, especially all this generative AI because now you can just throw all that stuff into a workload and then all of a sudden you'll get back a lot of the sentiment or all that kind stuff so you don't even to do the hard part anymore. Yeah, that's my rant.
turns.zh: 我觉得我对客户研究的看法，就像是85岁脾气暴躁的老头儿的观点。所以是这样的。在你的业务中，无论你经营什么类型的企业，一切都是为了推动客户完成转化，或者为你提供的产品或定价找到合理依据。而客户是活生生的人，你要引导他们达成转化目标，你的职责是了解他们如何看待你、如何看待他们自身的问题，以及如何看待周围的世界和你的产品。（00:41:00）：我们在理论层面都懂这些道理，但这里有一些有趣的数据。首先，仅有五分之一的公司有买家角色或理想客户画像（ICP）——只有五分之一！我们总在谈论这个话题，转发相关文章，提供建议，但看看我们自己的公司，只有五分之一有某种细分ICP。然后，仅有十分之一的公司每季度进行客户研究或开发。这本该是持续性工作，每月、每周都应该开展。但现实是，仅有十分之一的公司每季度做研究。也就是说，每月做研究的公司比例甚至更低。我觉得这太疯狂了。（00:41:44）：通过大量数据分析来看——我长期谈论客户开发的这个话题——一切都变得更好。NPS（净推荐值）更高，拥有客户开发职能（甚至只是ICP或买家角色，取决于你使用的框架）的组织NPS更高；客户支付意愿通常更高；销售漏斗更高效；LTV/CAC（客户终身价值/客户获取成本）通常高得多；增长数据方面，增长率通常更高，比如15%、20%，而非微不足道的增长幅度。客户留存率也更好。所有这些指标都更好了。（00:42:21）：我觉得20年前或10年前，你没必要做客户开发，因为——这就是基思[00:42:30模糊音]说客户研究是愚蠢之类的名言——那时没必要，因为市场竞争不激烈，我们都顺势而为。但现在市场环境越来越难了。那么你该怎么做？是继续撞南墙，还是真正去做我们都在谈论的客户研究？研究很难做到百分百准确，因为你必须运用判断力，但这就是你的职责。（00:42:54）：所以这更像是一次吐槽，而非深刻见解。但我也认为这正是人工智能开始解决的难题，尤其是生成式AI，因为现在你可以把所有数据输入工作负载，然后突然就能获取大量情感反馈等信息，这样你就不必再做那些繁琐的工作了。好吧，这就是我的吐槽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love the rant. Maybe one follow-up question. Why do you think it is that companies don't do this? I love the point you made of the retweeting, "Yeah, research is great." Writing blogs that research is use useful, "We've got to do research." Why do you think companies don't do it? And then what's one thing that maybe they could do tomorrow that'll bring them closer down that path?
turns.zh: 喜欢你这番吐槽。或许我能追问一个问题：你觉得为什么公司不这么做？你提到的转发推文很有意思，“是啊，研究很重要。” 写博客说研究有用，“我们必须做研究。” 但为什么公司不这么做呢？明天他们能做些什么来更接近这个目标？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: The one thing you can do, put a number on a whiteboard. You're going to have 10 customer conversations a month, just 10 non-sales conversations. You're just going to talk to 10 people. Or you're going to send one survey. And people are terrible at sending surveys. Surveys are actually great. You just have to be good at sending them. And good, it's not a high bar, it just means that you have 30 to 45 seconds of someone's time unless you're compensating them. And don't send 45-question surveys by email where the first question is, "What's your email?" Don't do that. But just put a number on the board. (00:44:09): I think the reason we don't do it is because it was, quote-unquote, "easy" to get away with not doing it. If you really think about a funded environment... and some products are so paradigm-shifting that the biggest misconception about customer research is I have to listen to them. You don't have to listen to them at all, you just have to understand where they are, and then you're filtering all of that with all this other data and then you're making a decision and you're earning your paycheck as a product person. Typically, it's the product person, but also in marketing. (00:44:37): So I think it's just one of those things where you could get away with not doing it. Now though, the way the market's going, you're just starting to see this more and more, you're starting to see more tooling. The reason you're seeing more tooling is because they're starting to connect it to actually being useful rather than you having to set up your own customer development program. I think the other reason typically people haven't had to do this is because there's a lot of brute forcing that's done in startup land and it only lasts so long. (00:45:06): So all of these companies that raise a bunch of money, get the $100 million dollar exit, everyone's clapping because it's a big number, but cap table screwed, everything's bad. It's a win because it's a win, but all of those companies are ones who were able to brute force to a certain level and they never learned how to actually understand their market or their customer. And I think that that kind of story will continue to happen as long as we have a lot of capital flowing in the market. But I would rather not be that company. I would rather be the company that gets the $100 million, 200 million exit with bootstrapping, or builds the billion-dollar annual revenue company because I know my market, I know my customer so well.
turns.zh: 你能做的一件事，就是在白板上写个数字。每个月进行10次非销售性质的客户对话，只需与10个人交流。或者发送一份调查问卷。但人们在发送调查问卷方面做得很糟糕。调查问卷其实很棒，只要能做好发送工作。做好发送并不需要高标准，只需确保对方有30到45秒的时间参与，除非你给他们报酬。别发那种45个问题的邮件调查，第一题就问“你的邮箱是什么？”千万别这么做。但就在白板上写个数字。（00:44:09）：我觉得我们不这么做的原因是，在资金充足的环境下……有些产品颠覆性太强，导致人们对客户研究最大的误解就是“必须听取他们的意见”。但其实根本不需要听取他们的意见，只需了解他们的现状，再结合其他数据进行分析，最后做出决策，凭借产品人的专业素养就能获得回报。通常是产品人员负责，但市场营销部门也一样。（00:44:37）：所以我认为这只是人们能逃避责任的一个借口。不过如今市场形势在变，相关工具越来越多了。工具之所以兴起，是因为它们开始与实际应用场景相结合，而不再需要单独搭建客户开发项目。我觉得人们不愿意做这件事的另一个原因是，初创公司常采用蛮力式方法，但这种方法只能持续一阵子。（00:45:06）：那些融资数亿美元、以高价退出市场的公司，人人都为之欢呼，但其实资本结构糟糕透顶。这是成功，但所有这类公司都是通过蛮力手段达到某种水平，却从未真正理解市场或客户。只要市场上资金充裕，这种情况就会持续下去。但我可不想成为那样的公司。我宁愿成为那种通过自力更生就能融资2亿美元、退出市场，年营收达数十亿美元的公司，因为我深知自己的市场和客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talking to customers is good, you should do it. Great reminder. People are going to listen to this like, "Yes, we should do this," and then we'll just move on. And then-
turns.zh: 和客户交流很棒，你应该这么做。提醒得真好。人们听完会点头说：“是啊，我们应该这么做”，然后就继续日常工作。然后——

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: My joke when I give talks is, "Only 20% of you are going to do this when I give a talk on it, and so I'm not even going to talk deeply on it. You 20%, come talk to me, I've got a whole framework for you," that type of a thing because I think people just nod their heads and they tweet it, and they just don't end up doing it.
turns.zh: 我做演讲时的玩笑是：“只有20%的人会在我讲完后真正行动，所以我甚至都懒得深入讲解。你们这20%，来找我吧，我为你们准备了完整框架。” 之类的，因为我觉得人们只是点头转发，却从不付诸行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Status quo is hard to overcome sometimes. We're onto our eighth topic, we've got three to go, and it's on competitive intelligence. And this touches on a really interesting part of your background that I don't know a lot of people know.
turns.zh: 现状有时确实难以突破。我们已经讲到第八个主题了，还剩三个主题要讲，今天要讲的是竞争情报。这部分内容涉及到你个人背景中一个非常有趣的部分，我相信很多人都不太了解。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah. So my background, I started my career... I worked in US Intelligence, I worked for NSA. And I was just a entry level intel analyst, basically, I was only there for just over a year. And what was interesting is you get taught first principles thinking in so many different ways because you're solving essentially puzzles every day. Now those puzzles are finding a bad guy or a gal or finding this piece of information. Those are all the puzzles, but you have to think through how to figure this out. And a lot of those puzzles involve, "You have these number of entities, how are they going to react?" And you're trying to predict how they're going to react, and you're also trying to help figure out how you're going to react or act in the context of them, so like node analysis, basically. (00:47:09): And what's interesting from a startup or a business perspective is I think that don't focus on your competitors is terrible advice. It's amazing advice for product teams. When you have a competitive intelligence program or you have competitive intel, I try never to share that with product ever because products should just focus on the customer, they should not give two craps what's going on with competitor A or competitor B. But as an overall missive, don't focus on your competitors is terrible advice. And if I'm being charitable, it's just outdated because some fun facts, and I alluded to some of them before, over the past decade, if you're building in tech, particularly in SaaS or subscriptions, you now have 16 times the number of competitors if you started a business today, than if you did 10 years ago, and this is because everyone and their mother can spin up a website, a server, they can drive traffic to that site. (00:48:02): So there's just a bunch of stuff in the market. And then because of all that stuff, all these marketing channels are getting denser and denser. CAC and B2B is up about 110% over the past 10 years. Consumer, it's up 145%. If you're selling sales and marketing software, it's up 220% because there's just so much sales and marketing software doing sales and marketing things in the market. And so the other reason for this is we haven't had a brand new marketing channel since 2015, and that was Snapchat. We have TikTok, but TBD, depending on how you think about it. But we're going from brand new marketing and advertising innovation every quarter to basically every five years. (00:48:42): My point is, if you are not in a Blue Ocean, you're not in the Peter Teal, go to a market of one, you're not in those types of things, which is most of us, and even some of us who think we're in those things, we're actually not, you do have to focus on your competitors on some level. And the levels I particularly think are a bare minimum, just knowing who they are, having a strategy. So for ProfitWell we never had comparison pages because we very quickly went from a challenger in this very competitive market to the leader in the market. So all of a sudden we were going to be above the fray, that was the idea, that was the strategy that we had, which is, "We're going to have a lot of intel on what's going on with them, why people care about this product." We had white label NPS surveys and customer development surveys going to our competitors' customers. That's the level. And it was just automated. It wasn't like it was taking a lot of time, but we just wanted that intel.
turns.zh:
是的。我的背景是，我开启职业生涯时……我在美国国家安全局（NSA）工作。当时我只是个初级情报分析师，基本只待了一年多时间。有趣的是，那里教会你用多种方式思考第一性原理，因为你每天都在解决各种难题。这些难题包括找出坏人或获取关键信息。核心挑战在于预测对手行为，并制定应对策略，比如节点分析之类的。  

从创业或商业视角看，别把精力放在竞争对手身上是个糟糕建议。这对产品团队倒是绝佳建议。但当你有竞争情报项目时，千万别和产品团队分享这些信息——产品团队只需专注客户，不必在意竞争对手动态。但从整体策略看，忽视竞争对手是不可取的。往好了说，这建议太过时了。过去十年，科技领域（尤其是SaaS和订阅模式）竞争环境发生巨变。如今创业者面对的竞争对手数量，是十年前的16倍。这是因为人人都能搭建网站、服务器，引流获客。  

（00:48:02）市场竞争激烈，客户获取成本（CAC）和B2B客户增长率近年来暴涨。消费者市场增长率达145%，销售营销软件领域更是飙升220%——市场上涌现大量同类产品。自2015年以来，我们再未见过全新营销渠道（比如Snapchat），TikTok前景尚不明朗。创新周期从季度级延长至五年级。  

关键在于：若不身处蓝海市场（如Peter Thiel提出的"一号市场"策略），多数创业者（包括自以为符合该策略者）都必须关注竞争对手。最基本策略包括：了解竞争对手、制定应对策略。  

以ProfitWell为例，我们从竞争者跃升为市场领导者后，迅速实施了竞争对手情报策略：通过白标NPS调查和客户发展调查，获取竞争对手客户数据。这些自动化操作虽耗时不多，但能获取关键洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say white labeled, that means you're emailing your competitor's customers to see what they think of your competitors, right?
turns.zh: 你们说的"白标行动"，意思是给竞争对手的客户发邮件，了解他们对竞争对手的看法，对吧？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Exactly. So we're basically, and we did it as a third party basically, which was, I think one of them was analyticssoftware.com, stuff like that. So it wasn't like we were spoofing as our competitor because I think that crosses a little bit of a line. But basically we would have this intel. There's a whole program here. Basically, I'd have sources... Basically, these customers I knew were always going to stay because they liked the founder or something like that. I would get on the phone with them every quarter or two just to be like, "Hey, what are you liking? Why haven't you switched yet?" these types of things, or I'd see them at conferences. (00:50:14): So there's a whole program there. And again, it's not like it's distracting anything, it's just I want the intel so I can predict what's going on, I can predict who to care about, who not to care about. But even then, if you're a challenger, competitor marketing pages are really powerful. And the thing is, your customers, especially in a denser market, they know your competitors exist or they're looking at them. Don't infantilize your customers, help them, "Hey, this is how we compare to X, Y, Z competitor," and be honest as much as possible. Well, we should always be honest, but be as upfront as possible, I should say, with where you're bad at and where you're great at, those types of things. (00:50:55): But long story short, having something awareness and then choosing a particular strategy, and then depending on your strategy, you might ramp up how much you actually do with the actual intelligence program.
turns.zh: 没错。所以我们基本上是以第三方的身份来做这件事。其中一个合作方是analyticssoftware.com之类的。但我们并没有冒充竞争对手，因为我觉得那样有点越界了。不过我们确实收集到了这些情报。这里有一套完整的方案。基本上，我有一些消息来源……那些客户我知道会一直留下来，因为他们喜欢创始人之类的。我每隔一两个季度就会和他们通电话，问问他们喜欢什么，为什么还没换掉平台之类的，或者在会议上和他们见面。（00:50:14）所以这是一套完整的方案。再说一次，这并没有造成任何干扰，我只是想获取这些情报，这样就能预测市场动态，判断哪些客户值得重点关注，哪些则不然。但即便如此，如果你是一家挑战者公司，竞争对手的营销页面其实非常有用。关键是，你的客户，尤其是那些身处竞争激烈市场的客户，他们都知道竞争对手的存在，或者正在关注竞争对手。别把客户想得太幼稚，应该帮助他们了解：“嘿，我们和X、Y、Z竞争对手的对比情况是这样的”，尽可能保持坦诚。当然，我们应该始终诚实，但我要说的是，要尽可能直白地指出自己在哪些方面做得好，哪些方面做得不好，诸如此类。（00:50:55）长话短说，先了解市场动态，再选择合适的策略，然后根据策略调整情报收集的力度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is amazing. Two questions. Should every startup have a former spy on their team to help them operationalize these ideas? And then two, is there anything else that you found super valuable that you did based on your training there?
turns.zh: 太棒了。两个问题。每个初创公司都应该在团队里安排一个前间谍来帮助他们将这些想法付诸实践吗？还有，基于你在那里的培训经历，你觉得还有哪些做法特别有价值？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: We didn't have a formal program, but I love hiring veterans, either veterans of intelligence, so they're citizens, so they're not veterans from a military perspective, but people who had worked in Intel or people who were actual veterans of different military branches. There's a lot of reasons for this, but I think that the intelligence folks, it's a way of thinking. Now you ought to be careful, and this is just purely my opinion, because depending on how long they were in... the reason I left is because it's the government, it's super bureaucratic. It was one of the most fulfilling jobs I will ever have, and I was only there for a short amount of time. But it's just one of those things where it's just so bureaucratic. (00:52:01): So the 15-year person there is not thriving, they're not trying to change the world necessarily. They have a job. So you've got to be careful with that. But yeah, I think there's these really smart people that just think in a different way. And a broader point is I think it's just really, really good to go to different industries. All this customer development stuff, you go to any major retailer or any major e-commerce company, they have entire teams just dedicated to this stuff. Hallmark was one of our first pricing customers back in the day before we went subscription focused. They had 119 people in customer insights and research. And this was one of the reason we were like, "Well, you guys don't need our help, you've got enough people." But those are great people to hire, even though they don't necessarily have the actual industry knowledge, they have a lot of domain expertise. (00:52:50): In terms of things I learned, I'll put it this way, not to get political, if I was in charge of budget, I would give so much more money into the intel community. I saw conflicts or heard about conflicts being stopped just because of intelligence that didn't go hot in terms of war fighting. I think it's one of those things where I would put so much more money there than the actual other side of the defense budget. (00:53:12): And also everyone asks me about Snowden. So again, not to get political, it's a lot more complicated, I think, than a lot of people think. It's one of those things that the issues that were brought up, obviously they got really sensationalized, but they're really important conversations to have, but it's not as simple as, "Oh, stop doing this, start doing that." (00:53:33): You don't have to worry about the NSA, the NSA's all outward-looking. You should worry about the FBI. The FBI are the ones who get a little testy with certain things, and you're seeing that in the court cases and stuff like that. But just know there's a lot of really hardworking, very well-intentioned people who you might disagree in terms of trade-offs, in terms of safety and things like that. They're also some of the most privacy orientated people on the planet, so that's worth a whole conversation. So hopefully I didn't throw too many grenades in this part.
turns.zh: 我们没有正式的项目，但我喜欢招聘退伍军人——无论是情报领域的退伍军人（他们毕竟是公民，所以从军事角度来看不算退伍军人），还是曾在情报机构工作过的人，或者来自不同军事分支的真正退伍军人。原因有很多，但我认为情报人员有一种独特的思维方式。现在你得小心些，这只是我的个人看法，因为他们在机构里待的时间长短不同……我离开的原因是政府部门太官僚了。那是我做过最充实的工作之一，但我在那里待的时间很短。但官僚作风实在太严重了。（00:52:01）所以一个有15年工作经验的人可能发展不顺，他们不一定想改变世界。他们只是在完成本职工作。所以你得谨慎考虑。不过我确实认为有些非常聪明的人思维方式与众不同。更宏观地说，我认为跨行业发展非常有益。比如客户开发这块，你去任何大型零售商或电商公司，他们都有专门的团队负责这项工作。早在我们转向订阅模式之前，Hallmark就是我们最早的定价客户之一。他们有119人专门从事客户洞察和研究工作。这让我们当时觉得：“嗯，你们不需要我们的帮助，人手已经够多了。” 但这些人才很值得聘用，即便他们不一定具备行业知识，他们也拥有丰富的专业领域经验。（00:52:50）至于我学到的经验，我这么说吧，不涉及政治。如果我负责预算，我会给情报界投入更多资金。我见过或听说过因为情报而避免了升级为战争的冲突。我认为在国防预算分配上，我们应该把更多资金投入情报领域，而不是其他方面。（00:53:12）还有，每个人都问我关于斯诺登的事。所以再说一次，不谈政治，这件事比很多人想象的要复杂得多。被提及的问题显然被过度炒作了，但这些对话非常重要，不能简单地说“哦，别这么做，改成那样做”。（00:53:33）你不用担心国家安全局（NSA），NSA更关注外部威胁。你应该担心联邦调查局（FBI）。FBI对某些事情会比较敏感，你从法庭案件之类的案例中就能看出来。总之，要知道有很多非常勤奋、善意的人，他们在权衡取舍、安全性等问题上可能与你意见不一致。他们也是地球上最注重隐私的人之一，这值得深入探讨。希望我在这部分没有说太多偏激的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, we need more grenades. That's the first time Snowden was brought up on this podcast, so that's cool. There you go. And this is actually a good segue to the next topic, which is around local strategies like FBI versus NSA. I think you have a strong perspective that local strategies are much more likely to [inaudible 00:54:19] so we'll just get into that one.
turns.zh: 不，我们需要更多偏激的观点。这是这个播客第一次提到斯诺登，很酷。继续吧。实际上这是一个很好的过渡到下一个话题的机会，即关于本地策略，比如FBI与NSA的对比。我认为你对本地策略更有见地，它们更有可能[00:54:19未听清]，所以我们就来探讨一下这个话题。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Just to give you a tease, I'll tell you what I think of Snowden after the podcast. So the world doesn't get to know except that I'll tell you what my opinion is afterwards.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。我先吊吊你们的胃口吧，等播客结束后我再告诉你们我对斯诺登的看法。这样全世界就不会知道了，只能等我之后跟你们说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a tease.
turns.zh: 真是个吊胃口的家伙。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Local strategies. Local strategies, very basic. People like to buy from people, but we as operators get so excited about the scale of the internet that we forget the basics of humanity. Here's some fun data points, we did a bunch of studies on this. So prospects who meet you in person, and this is not just for profit, all the data I've shared, it's all global-level data or segmented depending on how we did it. It's not just our findings, it's like we looked at probably a minimum of 2,000 companies per factoid and most of the time much more. But prospects who meet you in person have 10 to 30% higher willingness to pay than those who didn't. Churn for those folks who you meet in person is typically 20% lower than those folks who have never met you. Expansion revenue is typically 15 to 20% higher. (00:55:23): And this is not only in hand-to-hand kind of sales, coffee meetings, lunches, lunch and learns this type of thing, but it's also in scaled products, so products that cost 20, 50 bucks per month. And so my suggestion is to you, especially in a post-COVID, I don't know if that's the right term, but in a world that hopefully does not see another pandemic in our lifetimes, knock on wood, do meetups, do lunches, go to conferences, unless you're Lenny who is not a big fan of conferences. But get out of the office. Make sure you get out of the office. And the budget doesn't have to be as big as you think. Breakfast and lunches are super cheap. We would push all of our P2 and P3s to a meetup, and all of our P1s, we would have one-on-one coffee dates. It's super cheap.
turns.zh:
本地化策略。本地化策略，非常基础。人们喜欢从人那里购买产品，但我们作为运营者对互联网的规模太兴奋了，以至于忘记了人性最基本的法则。这里有一些有趣的数据点，我们对此做了很多研究。那么那些亲自见过你的人（这里不是指为了盈利），我分享的所有数据都是全球范围的，或者根据我们的研究方式进行细分。这些不仅仅是我们的发现，我们至少对每个数据点调查了2000家公司，大多数情况下调查的公司数量更多。但亲自见过你的人比没见过你的人愿意支付的价格高出10%到30%。见过你的人的客户流失率通常比从未见过你的人低20%。扩展收入通常高出15%到20%。
（00:55:23）：这不仅适用于面对面的销售，比如咖啡会面、午餐、午餐学习会等，还适用于标准化产品，比如每月20、50美元的产品。我的建议是，尤其是在后疫情时代，我不知道这个术语是否准确，但希望我们这辈子不再经历另一次大流行（但愿如此），参加聚会、共进午餐、参加会议，除非你像伦尼那样不喜欢会议。但一定要走出办公室。一定要走出办公室。预算不需要像你想象的那么大。早餐和午餐非常便宜。我们会把所有P2和P3级别的客户推向聚会，而所有P1级别的客户，我们会安排一对一的咖啡约会。费用很低。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do the Ps mean? Is that priority?
turns.zh: 这些P代表什么意思？是优先级吗？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Priority 1, we want these people to convert, they're very good fits, all this other stuff. P2s are like, they're probably good fits, but they're just not as big. And then P3s are with a content play, they just love our content and stuff, but they're not necessarily good fits for us. And so people make the mistake, they push everyone to dinners and it's like, I don't want to spend all of my money on P2s and P3s. (00:56:34): And so breakfast and lunches are cheaper than dinners. Meetups can be extremely inexpensive, get creative. We like to do barbecue type stuff for, not dive bars, but the unique dive bar, I guess is the best way to put it. So it's not fancy. People just want to meet people, they want to talk to you, especially if you're doing content and things like that. The Lenny Newsletter, Lenny Empire Meetups, I see the pictures of those all the time. There's just an urge to learn from one another and hang out. So yeah, that's the biggest thing, get out of the office or get out of your desk at home.
turns.zh:
优先级1，我们希望这些人能转化，他们非常合适，满足其他所有条件。P2级别的人可能也合适，但没那么合适。P3级别的人是通过内容吸引来的，他们喜欢我们的内容之类的，但对我们来说不一定合适。人们常犯的错误是把所有人都推向晚餐，而我不想把所有钱都花在P2和P3级别的人身上。
（00:56:34）：所以早餐和午餐比晚餐便宜。聚会可以非常便宜，发挥创意。比如我们喜欢做烧烤类型的活动，不是那种高档酒吧，而是那种独特的低调酒吧，我想这是最好的描述方式。所以不算高档。人们只是想见面、跟你聊天，尤其是如果你在做内容和类似的事情的话。伦尼通讯、伦尼帝国聚会，我经常看到这些照片。人们就是有一种互相学习、一起玩乐的冲动。是的，这才是最重要的，走出办公室或者走出家里的办公桌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. You're on Zoom. And you're saying it's not just the founders, it could be anyone on the team, salespeople, that all works.
turns.zh: 是啊，对啊。你现在在Zoom上呢。你说不只是创始人，团队里的任何人，销售人员都可以。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Anyone. I led marketing as part of my role as CEO, and so I do a lot of this and I'm also the one doing a lot of the content and stuff like that, or the face of a lot of our content, so I did a lot of it. But your head of sales... and you just have to position this a little differently. If they're going to meet with a salesperson, it's the same thing as if they get a email from a BDR, they're like, "I'm not going to figure it out. I don't want to deal with this." But if it's like, "Hey, we're hosting..." We're doing these lunch and learns right now. I was in Paris, New York, and London last week, it's probably why I'm so sick this week, and all of a sudden we did these lunch and learns. People just want to hang out. (00:57:47): So we had 10 people, we had 20 people at one, 10 people, all priority 1 leads. And then we did these meetups with 100-plus people at each. Just think of that brand equity. And you just hang out. It wasn't just me at all of these things. I ran the content, but then all of our sales folks were hanging out and doing their thing. But it doesn't have to be super complicated. It's just those touchpoints that people want. And it's so high leverage because there are a lot of people who will not answer your email but will come to an event to meet you or meet someone from your team because it's something to do, especially if you're buying them breakfast or coffee or something like that. It doesn't have to be something that's extravagant.
turns.zh: 任何人。作为首席执行官，我负责市场营销，所以我经常参与这项工作，同时我也负责很多内容创作之类的工作，还经常作为我们内容的代言人出镜，所以我做了很多这类事情。但你们的销售主管……你只需要稍微调整一下策略。如果他们要和销售人员会面，就像收到业务开发代表（BDR）发来的邮件一样，他们会想：“我不想费心思处理这些事。”但如果是说：“嘿，我们要举办……” 我们现在正在举办这些午餐学习会。上周我在巴黎、纽约和伦敦，这可能就是我这周生病的原因，突然之间我们就举办了这些午餐学习会。人们只是想聚一聚。（00:57:47）：所以我们有10人参加，一场活动有20人，都是优先级1的潜在客户。然后我们举办的聚会，每场都有100多人参加。想想那个品牌效应吧。而你只需要去参与。这些活动并非由我一人主导。我负责内容创作，但所有销售人员都会参与其中，和潜在客户交流互动。但这没必要太复杂。人们想要的只是那些能产生互动的接触点。因为这种高效的互动方式非常有价值，很多人不会回复你的邮件，但会来参加活动，与你或你的团队成员见面，因为这是一种社交方式，特别是如果你请他们吃早餐或咖啡之类的。不必搞得太铺张。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice. Basically, it's like if your sales aren't where you want it to be, find a way to meet your potential leads or someone in your team meeting your leads. That's a very actionable thing you could do like, "We're not hitting our numbers, let's just go meet some people, find opportunities to hang out in real life."
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种建议。基本上，如果你的销售业绩未达预期，那就想办法与潜在客户或团队成员见面。这是一个非常切实可行的做法，比如：“我们没达成销售目标，那就去见见人，找机会在现实中交流。”

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Well, in the early days, pre-product market fit, this is all we would do too. I would stay at the worst hotels, I would stay at hostels, but just to get to, "Okay, I want to sell to these people." The best information I'm going to get isn't in a Zoom or I'm asking them questions, it's going to be like, "Hey." I gave a talk on pricing because that was a high leverage thing I could do because no one knows anything about pricing, but they know it's important, so a lot of people want to listen. But then afterwards it's like, "Oh yeah, how do you think about this? What are you doing for this? What are you doing for..." all of those fun producty questions. It's just really, really high leverage. And I think it's one of those things that... It depends on your role, it depends on your stage, but everyone can use something there.
turns.zh: 嗯，在早期阶段，在产品市场契合度之前，我们也会这么做。我会住在最差的酒店，住青年旅社，但就是为了能接近目标客户：“好的，我要把产品卖给这些人。” 我能获取的最佳信息不在Zoom通话里，也不在问答环节里，而是通过直接交流。比如：“嘿。” 我做了一个关于定价的演讲，因为这是一个高效的策略，因为没人了解定价，但大家都知道定价很重要，所以很多人愿意听。但之后就是：“哦，对了，你怎么看待这个问题？你在这方面做了什么？” 这些有趣的产品相关问题。这真的非常高效。我认为无论你的角色或所处阶段如何，每个人都能从中受益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great segue to our final topic. A lot of people spend time on top of funnel driving visitors, driving traffic, getting the word out. A lot of people spend time at the end of the funnel, closing customers, increasing within an organization. You have this perspective that the middle of the funnel is maybe the biggest opportunity these days. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 很自然地过渡到我们最后的话题。很多人把时间花在前端，吸引访客、增加流量、宣传推广。很多人把时间花在后端，完成交易、在组织内推广。但你认为如今中端环节可能是最大的机遇。你能谈谈这一点吗？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Pound for pound biggest opportunity. So take a quick step back. Demand generation exists for more than just supporting the sales team. We forget that. So sales and marketing, the past decade, it's all been the funnel, we're top of the funnel, middle of funnel, bottom of the funnel. HubSpot's trying to make it a flywheel, but marketers are still talking about funnels. And when you look at the data, it depends a little bit on the price point and a little bit on the vertical, but 80% of sales and marketing budgets tend to go to the top of the funnel and the bottom of the funnel. So sales folks and ad-type spend, field events, whatever it is, that's where it goes. (01:00:24): And the whole point is you're trying to move someone from a lack of awareness at the top of the funnel to being aware about you and then to a sales combo or a conversion point, if you're not doing sales. The problem is bottom of the funnel efficiency and top of the funnel efficiency has plummeted the past decade, just plummeted. And it's not only because of the factoids I was saying before about CAC and all these other things and so many competitors being in the market, it's just one of those things that the days of just hiring a bunch of BDRs, not training them, not having them in account-based marketing, not doing all these other things, those days are not here anymore. Those days are gone. Maybe in some specific verticals, in specific parts of the market. (01:01:11): But here's the other problem. Sales today is so much more about timing than it once was. Because there's so much stuff out there, it's one of those things where people are waiting until it's the right time. They're aware of you, but they're waiting. So the question we have to ask ourselves to not bury the lead any further is do we need to make this river of demand generation, basically what demand generation works? But that's table space. (01:01:37): If we want to be even increasingly more successful, that middle of the funnel needs to get bigger. That pool of users who is aware of you, interacting with you on a regular basis. What if you had leads basically hanging out there in the middle of the funnel, interacting with you on a regular basis before all of a sudden their timing was right and then all of a sudden they go to the bottom of the funnel, and even better they opt into them. You don't have to keep going after them and doing sales processes that are very kind of churn and burn. So that pool of leads. (01:02:07): And so the best way to create pools of leads, freemium. I'm a huge fan of freemium. I used to write articles about how freemium is terrible, so I'm a big convert. I wrote a book on freemium as well. The thing with freemium is CAC is still up over the past decade, but it's up a lot less than overall CAC. Customers who convert from freemium and become paid customers, their retention is typically about 10 to 20% higher than those who converted from a free trial or converted from a traditional sales process. And then on top of that, NPS or CSAT, we measured it through NPS, is typically about double because they're converting on their own timeline, not on some artificial timeline of a free trial or artificial timeline of sales. (01:02:47): You should still have those things, but I want this pool of people who are aware of me and are using something of my product because at the end of the day, what better content do you have than your actual product? Even if you're a big enterprise solution, give them something to interact with. And then the other way to fill that middle of the funnel is, I think inbound marketing is just becoming SEO and eBooks. Kieran from HubSpot gets offended when I say that, but I love you, buddy. It's okay. I'm still a huge fan. And this is just because CAC and inbound marketing has gone up and it's all about a lot of SEO and we'll see what AI does to that. (01:03:21): But this whole thing of inbound media, we got on this train about five years ago, and inbound media is just podcast video series. When we sold the company, we had eight different podcasts and video series, all very niche like Pricing Page Tear Down, which was a show about we collected data and tore down pricing pages, the good and the bad. We had Boxed Out, which was a retention focused show for the subscription e-commerce industry. (01:03:44): So all of that was to build this pool so that people were aware of us. And then over time, all of a sudden they're like, "Oh, we have a pricing problem, we should go talk to these guys. Oh, we have this content or this retention thing, we should go talk to these guys." But I think the pool is kind of the future and a lot of people are still treating it as just this gateway between the top and the bottom of the funnel.
turns.zh:
按投入产出比衡量，最大的机遇就在这里。所以先退一步思考。需求生成的意义远不止于支持销售团队——我们常忽略这一点。过去十年，销售与营销部门一直专注于漏斗模型：顶部漏斗、中部漏斗、底部漏斗。HubSpot试图将其转变为飞轮模型，但多数营销人仍执着于漏斗思维。数据显示，无论价格区间或垂直领域如何，80%的营销预算往往流向漏斗顶部与底部——销售团队和广告投放、现场活动等投入无不如此。（01:00:24）关键在于，需求生成的核心任务是将潜在客户从漏斗顶部的无感知状态，引导至对品牌产生认知，再转化为销售线索或完成购买。问题在于过去十年中，漏斗顶部与底部的转化效率直线下滑。这不仅源于客户获取成本（CAC）等数据指标的变化，更因市场竞争加剧等多重因素。如今的销售更讲究时机把握——由于信息爆炸，客户往往选择时机成熟时再行动。因此，我们必须直面现实：传统漏斗模型已不适用。当前需求生成的核心在于——如何打造持续的用户池？（01:01:11）若想提升业绩，必须强化漏斗中部环节。即那些对品牌有认知、定期互动的用户群体。若能让这些潜在客户在时机成熟前长期沉浸于产品互动，最终自然转化为付费用户，效果将更为显著。（01:02:07）免费增值模式（freemium）是构建用户池的最佳路径。我曾撰文批判其弊端，如今却深信其价值，甚至写了一本相关著作。数据显示，尽管CAC在过去十年间持续攀升，但增量远低于整体CAC。通过免费试用转化为付费用户的客户，其留存率通常比传统销售流程高出20%以上。同时，NPS或CSAT等指标因用户自主决策而显著提升。（01:02:47）这些数据固然重要，但更关键的是：如何建立对品牌有认知、持续使用产品的用户群体？毕竟，最优质的内容莫过于产品本身。即便面对大型企业解决方案，提供互动体验同样重要。填补漏斗中部的关键在于：
我觉得入境营销现在就剩下SEO和电子书了。HubSpot的基兰听到我这么说会生气，但老兄，我爱你啊。这没关系，我还是你的超级粉丝。只是因为客户获取成本（CAC）和入境营销的成本越来越高，导致大家都把注意力转向SEO了，而人工智能会让这方面发生变革。（01:03:21）但说回入境媒体这事，我们五年前就开始布局了，当时主要就是播客和视频系列。公司被卖掉的时候，我们有八个不同的播客和视频系列，内容都非常垂直，比如《定价页面解析》——这是一档收集数据、拆解定价页面优劣的节目；还有《订阅电商行业留存指南》——《Boxed Out》等节目。（01:03:44）这些内容都是为了建立我们的品牌知名度。随着时间推移，人们突然发现：“哦，我们有定价难题，该找他们聊聊。”“哦，我们需要这方面的内容或留存策略，该找他们帮忙。”但我觉得品牌池才是未来，可惜很多人还是把它当作从漏斗顶部到底部的过渡环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Middle of the funnel is the new top of funnel. We need a bumper sticker.
turns.zh: 漏斗中段才是新的“漏斗顶部”。我们需要一个保险杠贴纸。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: There you go. I don't know if that's going to sell well, but I will buy one, so.
turns.zh: 好的，我不知道这玩意儿能不能卖得好，但我会买一个，所以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The most nerdiest of all bumper stickers. Patrick, we've gone through 10 topics. Is there anything else you want to touch on before we get to our very exciting lightning rounds?
turns.zh: 这是最书呆子气的保险杠贴纸。帕特里克，我们已经讨论了10个话题了。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想聊的吗？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I think what I will say is this is all still hard. So I'm giving some heuristics, I'm giving some benchmarks, but your mileage is going to vary. But again, that's your job, whether you're a founder, a product person, an exec, whatever you are, your job is to take in information, your job is to analyze the problem, and then ultimately come up with the best solution. And so I think it's one of those things that there's some hard truths I think we talked about, but then there's a lot of this that you have to evaluate it for yourself. So just a general, I may come off like a know-it-all, but I understand that mileage varies I guess is the best way...
turns.zh: 我觉得这一切还是挺难的。所以我给出一些启发，提供一些基准，但效果因人而异。不过话说回来，这就是你的工作，无论你是创始人、产品经理、执行官，还是其他什么角色，你的职责就是吸收信息，分析问题，最终找到最佳解决方案。所以我觉得有些事情虽然我们已经谈过了一些硬道理，但很多时候还是需要你自己去评估。所以总的来说，我可能显得很自以为是，但我理解各人有各人的情况——这或许是最好的说法……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，现在我们要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我有六个问题要问你们。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I feel like I need a buzzer.
turns.zh: 我感觉我需要一个抢答器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to add a buzzer someday. Anyway, here we go. What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 我总有一天会加个抢答器的。不管怎样，开始吧。你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I have read High Output Management probably 20 times in the past 10 years. I read it at least once a year now. I commissioned a bronze bust of Andy Grove, so that's being done. I'm a big Andy Grove fan.
turns.zh: 过去10年里，我大概读了20遍《高效能人士的七个习惯》了。现在我每年至少读一遍。我委托人制作了一个安迪·格鲁夫的青铜半身像，现在正在制作中。我是安迪·格鲁夫的超级粉丝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, it's in progress?
turns.zh: 哦，正在制作中？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah. It's in progress. It's not done. I'll send you a mockup after this. But yeah, High Output Management. Thinking in Bets, going to that first principles thinking. I find that a good book to share with people so that they can think about things and get on board with that. (01:05:40): And then Powerful by Patty McCord. Anything around HR to kind of break your brain a little bit about what you think about HR and people ops. That's the gateway drug. That was the one where I was like, "Oh, we can choose how to design our people ops teams."
turns.zh: 是的，是的，是的。还在制作中。还没完成。等会儿我会给你们发个模型。不过是的，《高效能人士的七个习惯》。《用概率思考》，也是遵循第一性原理的思维方式。我觉得这本书很适合分享给别人，让他们能思考问题并接受这种思维方式。（01:05:40）：然后是帕蒂·麦考德的《权力》。这本书涉及人力资源领域，能让人对人力资源和人员运营有新的认识。这本书让我意识到，我们可以自主设计人力资源团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, next question. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 好的，下一个问题。最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I don't have one that's recent, but I watch The West Wing at least once per week, so I've done that for a long time. I love Sorkin, I think the writing's just so good, so I'll just throw that out.
turns.zh: 我最近没有特别喜欢的，但我每周至少看一次《白宫风云》，我已经坚持很久了。我喜欢索金，他写的剧本太棒了，所以就提一下吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great one. Someone was telling me there's a podcast to analyze each episode, which [inaudible 01:06:14].
turns.zh: 很棒的。有人告诉我有个播客会分析每集内容，[音频中断01:06:14]。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: It is a great podcast and I've listened to most of them, so yeah.
turns.zh: 那是个很棒的播客，我听过大部分内容，所以是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. You're all over it. Favorite interview question that you like to ask because you're interviewing.
turns.zh: 好的，很棒。你们都懂了。你最喜欢问的面试问题，因为你自己也在面试别人。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I have a controversial one. I'm not going to be able to go through the entire question in a lightning round. But what I do is I do a mini... I did all the final interviews at ProfitWell, and we did a very hard culture check in the final interview. There's a mini case study, it only lasts about a couple of minutes, I'm not going to go through it, but I asked them if someone in Slack responded to someone sharing something benign, like some report they found on the internet from McKinsey, they shared it in Slack, and then someone responded to that with something indirectly offensive. (01:06:55): So it's changed over the years, sometimes I say, "Oh, they called it the R word, they said it was stupid," something indirectly offensive. And I say, "What would you do, and what do you think the company should do?" And no matter what they say, I challenge them, and I always tell them, "I've never seen that at ProfitWell," which is always good just to make sure they don't have a bunch of fear in this position. (01:07:19): But it gave me a really, really good opportunity to talk through our culture, particularly the most charitable interpretation piece. And I would say there were about 10% of people who had a zero tolerance policy for whatever the situation was. And I would tell them, I would say, "Hey, listen. We have zero tolerance for the obvious things, we probably all agree on those." But for this type of situation, we would ask some questions, we'd want to figure it out, we want to see, there's probably some judgment around what happened, how long if they'd been doing this for a while, that type of thing. And then we would make a decision on what would happen. And a lot of times nothing would happen except, "Hey, don't be an idiot, you're smarter than that, use better words," or something like that. And so that was a good culture check to opt them in or out.
turns.zh: 我有个比较有争议的问题。我没法在快速问答环节把整个问题都讲完。但我的做法是做一个简短的……我在ProfitWell负责所有的终面面试，我们在终面环节会做一个非常严格的文化筛选。会有一个简短的案例分析，通常只持续几分钟，我就不详细讲了。但我会问他们，比如在Slack上有人回复别人分享的东西，比如麦肯锡的某份报告，然后有人用带有隐晦攻击性的言论回复。（01:06:55）：这些年来情况有所变化，有时我会说：“哦，他们用了那个带有歧义的词，说这很愚蠢”，或者类似的带有攻击性的言论。我会问他们：“你会怎么做？你认为公司应该怎么做？”无论他们怎么回答，我都会反驳他们，并且总是告诉他们：“我在ProfitWell从未见过这种情况。”这样做能确保他们不会对这个职位心怀恐惧。（01:07:19）：但这给了我一个绝佳的机会来深入探讨我们的企业文化，尤其是最宽容的解读部分。我发现约有10%的人对任何情况都采取零容忍政策。我会告诉他们：“嘿，听着。我们对显而易见的事情零容忍，这点大家应该都认同。”但对于这类情况，我们会先进行调查，了解具体情况，比如事件持续了多久，行为是否反复发生等等。然后再决定如何处理。通常除了说“别犯傻，你应该更明智些，用词要恰当”之类的话外，不会有其他处罚。这次文化筛选很有效，能帮我们筛选出合适的人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is very cool. It circles back to the value of culture and values and being aligned within your company on culture and values. And it's interesting that that's the question you ask, and not something technical or skill-based.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。这又回到了文化和价值观的价值，以及在公司内部保持文化和价值观一致的重要性。有趣的是，你问的这个问题不是技术性或基于技能的，而是关于文化的。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I do all the final interviews. So they've already gone through a skill-based and they've done culture screen already and stuff like that. So this is more of the, here's why you should not work here, that type of conversation basically.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，我负责所有的终面面试。所以他们已经经过了技能测试和文化筛选之类的环节。所以这更多的是告诉他们为什么不应该来这里工作，类似这样的对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Next question, what are five SaaS products that you or your company uses that you love? And bonus points for ones maybe people haven't heard,
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个问题。下一个问题，请列出你或你的公司使用的五个SaaS产品，并说出你喜欢它们的原因。若能推荐一些大家可能没听说过的产品，那就更好了。

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: That's hard to answer too because at the end of the day, we'd all say Zoom, Google Workspace or whatever they're calling it these days because those are the things that are so central. I've got to give a shout-out to Notion, we use Notion for all of our documentation. I use Notion for my personal... all these things. I know Code is a sponsor, so I apologize but-
turns.zh: 这也很难回答，因为说到底，我们都会说Zoom、Google Workspace之类的，因为这些工具太核心了。我得特别提一下Notion，我们用Notion做所有文档管理。我个人也用Notion做各种事务。我知道Code是赞助商，所以很抱歉，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're both sponsors, and so we're friends with everyone over here. Both are great-
turns.zh: 他们都是赞助商，所以我们和这里的每个人都是朋友。两家公司都很棒——

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: Amazing. Lenny's Podcast, friends of all products. Descript. I use Descript quite a bit. I use Descript not only for... it's like a video recording and editing tool, or you can bring in video to edit. But it's got some cool features that... I use it more than Loom a lot of times because it just works in my workflow, not only for creating, but also for those quick conversations. (01:09:25): K-Tool. Here's a fun one. This is an indie product, K-Tool. There's probably other products that exist like this, but I actually really like the interface of it, it's super simple. Basically if I'm online or someone sends me a PDF or something like that, I can basically choose to send that to my Kindle. So if someone sends me something I could just choose to send and then I can batch all of those things into a weekly newsletter that I can curate. So my Sundays and my Monday morning are just spent reading. So I have this weekly newsletter of someone wants me to review this thing or someone wants me to read this article or something like that. So I batch that into a little newsletter and it's just a Chrome extension that works really well. (01:10:03): Tweet Hunter, I'm trying to be more on Twitter. I went through lulls, so now I'm trying to be consistent. So Tweet Hunter's pretty good. It's got some AI fun stuff into it to make discovery better. And then it's not a SaaS application, but the last one is this Apple Watch Ultra. So I don't carry my phone anymore. I just don't... I found myself being on a computer, walking away with my phone, going, doing stuff and then just never being off-screen. So I have this for when I'm not in front of my computer and I'm this close to also doing it when I travel to when I've been traveling, my phone will stay in my suitcase, but it connects if I need to make a phone call. It connects via Bluetooth, all that kind of stuff. But just trying to take my attention away from my phone basically, so that's, that's been the unlock.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Lenny的播客，所有产品的爱好者。Descript。我经常使用Descript。它不仅是一个视频录制和编辑工具，还能导入视频进行剪辑。但它有一些很酷的功能……我用它比用Loom多得多，因为它完全融入了我的工作流程——不仅用于创作，还能用于快速沟通。（01:09:25）：K-Tool。这是一个有趣的工具。这是一款独立产品，K-Tool。可能还有其他类似的产品，但我真的很喜欢它的界面，超级简单。基本上，如果我在网上，或者有人发给我PDF文件之类的，我可以选择发送到我的Kindle上。这样如果有人发给我东西，我只需选择发送，然后就能把所有这些内容整理成每周通讯。我周日和周一早上就花时间阅读这些内容。比如有人让我评论某个产品，或者读一篇文章之类的。我把这些内容整合成小通讯，这只是一个运行良好的Chrome扩展程序。（01:10:03）：Tweet Hunter，我在努力更频繁地使用Twitter。我经历过低谷期，现在正努力保持一致性。Tweet Hunter很不错。它加入了一些AI功能来优化内容发现。最后一款是Apple Watch Ultra。我不再随身携带手机了。我发现自己在电脑前时，手机可能还在充电或者其他地方，根本没法脱离屏幕。所以当我不在电脑前时，我会用它。旅行时，我也会用它。我的手机会留在行李箱里，但需要打电话时还能连接。通过蓝牙连接之类的。总之，就是想把注意力从手机上转移开，这才是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Damn. What a list. That was incredible. I'm going to ask just one more question. What's favorite lesson from your NSA experience that helps you in life day to day?
turns.zh: 天哪。真是个长长的清单。太棒了。我再问一个问题。你从NSA经历中学到的最有用的日常生活经验是什么？

turns.speaker: Patrick Campbell
turns.en: I shouldn't say everything, but most things are more complicated than it seems. And that's not like a sinister thing, it just means when that person's coming at you and super angry about something, whether it's your fault or not, something's there, they're having a bad day, on top of it, you really messed up, you tapped into a particular emotion that you didn't realize you did. Or hey, there's even the story in the news about this politician's bad or something like that. Everything's a lot more complicated, and not in a it's too hard to understand way, it's just you should always caution yourself on believing the first reaction that you have. (01:11:44): And I developed that there because there's so many things where... And it was also my first job, so a lot of this stuff happens because it's your first job, many people may have this experience at a different place, but it was like, "Oh, this geopolitical thing that's happened. Oh, here's my first instinct, that means this is bad." They're like, "Well, actually, there's this other thing going on over here and this other thing going over there, and those are actually connected. That's why this is caused." So that's helped me, one, not get so pissed off at the news. That's also helped me, I think just as a human, along with most charitable interpretation, to just be like, "Okay, let me not overreact here. Let me seek to understand and then react or respond, versus react."
turns.zh: 我不该把一切都说出来，但大多数事情比表面看起来要复杂得多。这倒不是什么坏事，只是当那个人冲你发火，无论问题是否因你而起，总归是另有隐情——他们当天心情不佳，而你又恰好做错了事，还触动了对方未曾察觉的情绪。或者想想新闻里那位政客的丑闻。所有事情都远比表面复杂得多，并非难以理解，而是你永远不能轻信自己的第一反应。（01:11:44）这让我意识到，许多时候……这也是我的第一份工作，所以很多情况都是因为初入职场导致的。很多人可能在其他地方有过类似经历，但当时的反应往往是“哦，某个地缘政治事件发生了。哦，我的第一反应是这很糟糕。”而对方会说：“其实还有其他因素在起作用，这些因素相互关联。这才是问题的根源。”这让我学会了两件事：一是不再对新闻过度愤怒；二是以最善意的解读去理解他人，而非冲动反应。

turns.en: What a beautiful way to end it. Patrick Campbell, renaissance man of a brain. This may be the most action-packed episode we've had, and I'm not surprised. Two final questions where can folks find you online if they want to ask you questions, reach out, learn more about what you're up to? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 多么完美的收尾。帕特里克·坎贝尔，堪称智力全才。这可能是我们节目中最精彩的一集，我并不意外。最后两个问题：如果听众想向你提问、联系你，或者想了解更多信息，可以在哪里找到你？听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.en: Yeah, so I am on Twitter @patticus, childhood nickname, P-A-T-T-I-C-U-S. LinkedIn, Patrick Campbell. I don't check my LinkedIn messages, I'm going to get around to it, it's just there's so much spam in there. But yeah, you could find me there or just pc@patticus.com, that's my personal email. So yeah, if I can be helpful or you want to see more of the data or you have this question or that question, we've probably written or recorded something on some of the things we talked about today, so I'm happy to send it over and just obviously want to be helpful, so yeah, feel free to hit me up.
turns.zh: 是的，我在推特上@patticus，这是我的童年昵称 P-A-T-T-I-C-U-S。领英账号是Patrick Campbell。我不怎么看领英消息，不过会处理的，只是里面太多垃圾信息了。不过你可以在那里找到我，或者发邮件至pc@patticus.com，这是我的个人邮箱。所以如果我能帮到忙，或者你想查看更多数据，或者有任何问题，今天我们谈论的很多内容都已写成文章或录制成播客，我很乐意分享。总之，随时联系我。

turns.en: Amazing. Patrick, thank you again for being here.
